input.title: Depesza  attache wojskowego w Rydze
input.summary: This document consists of military correspondence from October 1920, transmitted by the Polish General Staff's Second Division to the General Adjutancy of the Supreme Commander. It contains transcripts of telegrams from the Polish military attaché in Riga (Myszkowski), reporting on the situation facing the Polish population in Lithuania following General Żeligowski's military action. The telegrams describe the Lithuanian government conducting anti-Polish agitation in the Sejm and official press, arresting Poles, suppressing the Polish language, and organizing paramilitary riflemen's associations modeled on Bolshevik-style units to act against Poles. The Polish delegate from Kovno is demanding an ultimatum requiring Lithuania to halt these activities, dissolve the riflemen's organizations, and release political prisoners. The attaché warns that if Żeligowski's action does not expand to cover all of Lithuania, it risks leading to mass pogroms against the Polish population.

input.title: List do Instrukcji dla delegacji do Baranowcz i Berdyczowa.
input.summary: This document consists of official military correspondence from the Supreme Command of the Polish Armed Forces (General Staff), dated October 1920. It is addressed to the General Adjutancy and includes an enclosed copy of instructions for delegations to Baranowicze and Berdychiv. The document is signed by Lieutenant Colonel Matuszewski, acting on behalf of the Chief of Section II (Intelligence). A reference number and field post markings indicate it was handled through military postal channels during the Polish-Soviet War period. The original document is archived at the Pilsudski Institute in New York.

input.title: Sześć listów kapitana hrabiego Morstina z Paryża do generała Rozwadowskiego wraz 27 numerem gazety "Temps"
input.summary: These documents are letters from Count Morsztyn, written from Paris in July and August 1920, addressed to a Polish General, likely during the Polish-Soviet War. The correspondence covers diplomatic and military affairs, including press reports of tensions between General Weygand and the Polish Supreme Commander, which Morsztyn believed were being exploited by Britain to undermine confidence in Poland's ability to defend itself. Morsztyn reports on Allied attitudes toward potential armistice negotiations with the Bolsheviks, noting that French Marshal Foch was monitoring the situation and prepared to intervene if no armistice was reached. The letters also address disputes over the territories of Spisz, Orawa, and Cieszyn, the question of Danzig, and the difficulties of coordinating Polish diplomatic efforts in Paris, including criticism of certain Polish representatives whose conduct was damaging negotiations with France.

input.title: Informacja o zmianach po dymisji ministra Lefevre'a
O trzeźwość w ocenie sytuacji
input.summary: This document, dated 1962, is from a reader's corner section of a Polish-language publication, which welcomes reader correspondence while noting that submitted opinions represent personal views and not necessarily those of the editorial board. The editorial guidelines request that contributors write on one side of the paper only, leave a left margin, and write clearly. The main article, titled "On Sobriety in Assessing the Situation" by Jerzy Boleszczyk-Zakrzewski, discusses historical Polish-Russian and Polish-Ukrainian conflicts, referencing events from 1917, 1921, and 1939–1945. The author argues that conflicts along Poland's eastern borders, involving Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine, were natural consequences of ongoing bloody struggles against Moscow's expansionism and the fight for national independence.

input.title: Plany Watykanu dotyczące stworzenia związku państw katolickich

Wiadomości Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej wysłane z Polski 8 lutego 1938
input.summary: Admiral Miklós Horthy, Regent of Hungary, visited Poland starting Saturday, February 5, 1938. Horthy is recognized as a national hero who saved Hungary from communism in the tragic post-war period of 1918 and has led the country's reconstruction for 15-20 years. The visit was characterized as a state visit rather than a ceremonial celebration, reflecting the deep historical ties between Hungary and Poland that date back centuries to the times of Queen Jadwiga and King Stefan Batory. Under Horthy's leadership, successive Hungarian governments have implemented important social, economic, and constitutional reforms. Poland warmly received the Hungarian Regent at Wawel Castle, symbolizing the strong relationship between the two nations.

input.title: Serwis lotniczy Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej-List nr 17
input.summary: The document describes Hungarian Regent Admiral Miklós Horthy's state visit to Poland beginning February 5, 1938. The visit highlights the centuries-old friendship between Poland and Hungary, with no historical conflicts between the neighboring nations despite their long shared border. Horthy arrived in Kraków where he was ceremonially welcomed by Polish President Mościcki at the royal Wawel Castle, laid wreaths at Marshal Piłsudski's crypt and King Stefan Batory's tomb, and stayed in restored royal apartments. During an official dinner, both leaders exchanged toasts emphasizing the deep historical bonds, shared values, and cultural similarities between their two nations.

input.title: Insygnia Królewskie
input.summary: This document concerns the investigation into Polish royal regalia (crown jewels) believed to be hidden in a church in Volodymyr-Volynskyi (Włodzimierz Wołyński). In 1920, the Military Minister Sosnkowski dispatched Professor Gembarzewski and Captain Żmigrodzki to search for the regalia based on intelligence suggesting they had been hidden there since 1794, when a Capuchin friar allegedly concealed the crowns, scepters, and other royal insignia within the monastery. The search ultimately failed to locate the treasures, prompting debate in the Parliamentary Military Commission about the credibility of the official report. Minister Sosnkowski subsequently proposed forming a commission of five to seven respected individuals to review the evidence and testimony, while keeping sensitive details secret so as not to hinder future searches. Correspondence was exchanged between the Minister, the President of Ministers, the Marshal of the Sejm, Bishop Dubowski, and other officials to address lingering doubts about how the investigation was conducted.

input.title: Rzecznik, obrońca i realizator demokracji
input.summary: The document appears to be a Polish-language biographical retrospective describing an individual's career beginning after a "Roman revolution" in 1917, when he worked as a legal consultant. He subsequently held roles as a justice for Italy and allied states in 1918, a university professor and economic affairs chairman in 1919, and escalated to president of economic affairs for all allied nations from 1920 onward. The remainder of the document repetitively lists his role as president of economic affairs for all allied states during the months of November and December for each successive year from 1920 through at least 1980, with no variation in the description.

input.title: Odpowiedzi Wolnej Kozaczczyzny- zbiór artykułów polemicznych skierowanych do generała Bohajewskiego. Praga. 1929.
input.summary: The document contrasts the Russian and Cossack émigré communities, arguing that Cossacks have a natural affinity for agricultural labor and a genuine desire to return to and liberate their homeland, while Russian émigrés prefer intellectual pursuits, endless political debate, and the passive awaiting of Soviet collapse. Russian émigré leaders are accused of deliberately undermining Cossack settlement opportunities abroad to keep Cossacks available as a military force for their own political ambitions. Don Ataman Bogaevsky is criticized for subordinating Cossack interests to the goal of restoring a unified Russia centered on Moscow, remaining indifferent to the suffering of Cossacks both in exile and on the Don. The document praises the Ukrainian émigré community as a model of productive exile activity—establishing schools, scientific institutions, and trained cadres—and laments that after nine years abroad, Cossack leadership has produced virtually nothing comparable despite having had significant resources at its disposal.

input.title: W obronie marszałka - Józef Piłsudski według prof. Zbigniewa Wójcika
input.summary: Professor Zbigniew Wójcik, who had a personal connection to Józef Piłsudski as the son of a gendarme who served the Marshal, has written a short biographical sketch titled "Józef Piłsudski 1867–1935" as a defense against what he considers slanderous attacks on Piłsudski's legacy. The book addresses common criticisms of Piłsudski, including his association with socialism, his cooperation with German and Austro-Hungarian forces, his collaboration with foreign intelligence, and accusations of treason during the 1920 Battle of Warsaw, arguing that these actions were justified by the overriding goal of Polish independence. Wójcik also defends the May Coup of 1926, rejecting the characterization of it as a "crime" by drawing comparisons to other historical leaders who seized power by force, while acknowledging that Piłsudski's treatment of political opponents in his later years was difficult to fully justify. Despite these criticisms, Wójcik concludes that Piłsudski's flaws cannot overshadow his monumental contributions as the primary architect of the restored Polish state and the leader who achieved Poland's greatest military victory since 1683.

input.title: Pismo przewodnie do Ministerstwa Spraw Zagranicznych dotyczące wysyłki wycinków z prasy Ekwadoru wraz z załącznikami
input.summary: The Polish Embassy in Brazil forwarded press clippings from Ecuador dated May-June 1929 to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Warsaw. The main article from "Diario del Pueblo" reports that Poland, with a population of 30 million and facing emigration pressures, aspires to obtain colonial territories in Central Africa. The article states that Poland, along with Germany, Italy, and Japan, plans to request colonial mandates when the League of Nations reviews the colonial distributions from 1919 at its 1929 session. Poland claims the right to demand a portion of former German colonies, specifically seeking approximately 100,000 square kilometers in Central Africa.

input.title: Projekt umowy między Polską a Ukrainą.
input.summary: This document is a draft treaty between Poland and the Ukrainian People's Republic, dated April 15, 1920, in which Poland recognizes the Ukrainian Directorate government led by Symon Petliura as the de facto government of Ukraine. The agreement establishes borders between the two states along the Zbruch River and certain administrative boundaries, with Poland committing to transfer to Ukraine territories it holds or may recover from the Bolsheviks up to Poland's pre-partition borders of 1772. Ukraine in turn pledges not to conclude any international agreements directed against Poland and not to negotiate peace with the Bolsheviks without Polish consent. The treaty also provides for reciprocal national and cultural rights for Polish citizens in Ukraine and Ukrainian citizens in Poland, as well as separate economic and military conventions to be concluded as integral parts of the agreement. The entire treaty was to remain secret and could not be shared with third parties or published without mutual consent from both contracting parties.

input.title: Prace Podkomisji Politycznej Konferencji Polsko-Fińskiej
input.summary: This document records the proceedings of the Political Subcommission of the Polish-Finnish Conference in March 1920, attended by senior diplomats and officials from both countries. The two parties agreed to maintain absolute secrecy over their deliberations and to inform the Allied Powers of any peace-related decisions only as a formality through normal diplomatic channels. Finland committed not to pursue separate peace negotiations with Soviet Russia, leaving Poland to initiate or set the terms of any peace offers, while both nations pledged to mutually support each other's territorial claims. Finland sought self-determination for Karelia, access to the Arctic Ocean, minority rights for Ingrian Finns, and neutralization of the Gulf of Finland, while Poland demanded the reversal of the 18th-century partitions and the return of territories annexed by Russia since 1772. Additionally, Poland stipulated that it would not negotiate peace with Soviet Russia unless Finland was invited to participate and Russia first formally recognized Finnish independence.

input.title: Litwa Kowieńska wobec rokowań pokojowych
input.summary: This document, authored by M. Świechowski and dated June 6, 1920, is a memorandum analyzing the difficult diplomatic position Poland faced regarding Kaunas Lithuania during peace negotiations with Soviet Russia. The author warns that the Bolsheviks would likely exploit the Polish-Lithuanian dispute by demanding recognition of the Kaunas Lithuanian state as a condition for accepting the 1772 borders, which could isolate Poland diplomatically in European opinion and cause internal divisions within the Polish peace delegation. Świechowski argues that allowing the situation to drag on risked a permanent Russian-German corridor flanking Poland from the north, the marginalization of Polish populations in the Kaunas region, and the ultimate failure of Poland's broader eastern federalist program. As a solution, he proposes swift armed intervention to remove the Taryba government before peace talks begin and before the Kaunas Sejm convenes, presenting it as a fait accompli while offering concessions to Britain to soften international backlash. The memorandum concludes that Poland must decide immediately whether its federalist program is genuine policy or mere decoration, warning that delay would make such action impossible and lead to Poland's moral and political defeat on the Lithuanian question.

input.title: Polska ofensywa
input.summary: This document, dated May 18, 1920, is an official communication from the Polish Supreme Command to the General Adjutancy, summarizing a published letter written by Russian General Brusilov to the Chief of the All-Russian General Staff during the Polish offensive. In the letter, Brusilov acknowledges Polish military advances and suggests they may be aimed at reclaiming territories belonging to pre-1772 Poland, calling for a council of experienced military commanders to assess Russia's situation. He argues that while free Russia was right to liberate the Polish people and allow them self-determination, Poland has no right to invade lands historically belonging to the Russian nation, and that such aggression must be repelled by force. The document was signed by General Haller, Acting Chief of the General Staff, and is archived at the Piłsudski Institute in New York.

input.title: List do Komendanta
input.summary: This document is a letter dated May 12, 1920, from Warsaw, addressed to "Kochany Komendancie" (Dear Commander), likely Polish Chief of State Józef Piłsudski. The author reports on a series of visits from Hungarian representatives acting on behalf of Admiral Horthy, who proposed close Polish-Hungarian cooperation, including a planned Slovak uprising against Czechoslovakia involving over 30,000 insurgents backed by the Hungarian army, with requests for Polish territory to be used as a staging ground and for weapons transport via Polish railways. The author outlines his cautious responses to these proposals, citing Poland's ongoing war in the East and the risk of international complications, offering instead a policy of "benevolent neutrality" and conditional assistance with arms smuggling. The letter also discusses Hungary's request for Polish diplomatic intervention with Romania to ensure Romanian neutrality during the planned Hungarian western operation. Additionally, the author describes a concerning development with the French military mission, noting that France was now conditioning further arms and ammunition deliveries on barter trade, which he interprets as an attempt to pressure Poland into accepting France as an equal partner in Ukrainian affairs.

input.title: Dokumenty dotyczące  Legionów w okresie poprzysięgowym
input.summary: This document is a Polish-language article written by Colonel Rydz-Śmigły, published on August 29, 1917, in a pamphlet titled *W Dzisiejszej Chwili* (In This Moment), drawn from the Archive of Marshal Józef Piłsudski. The article discusses the crisis surrounding the Polish Legions following the oath crisis, during which thousands of Polish soldiers and officers were interned in camps such as Szczypiorno and Beniaminów for refusing to swear allegiance to foreign military authorities, including German General Beseler. The author strongly criticizes the Legion Command for suppressing the national character of the Legions and for acting against the interests of Polish independence by enforcing the oath and removing so-called "Piłsudski supporters" from the ranks. The article argues that it was precisely these "Piłsudczycy" (Piłsudski loyalists) who had consistently fought to secure the Legions' Polish identity, autonomy, and dignity against both Austrian and German military authority. The text frames the internment of these soldiers as a profound betrayal of the ideals for which the Legions were originally founded.

input.title: List premiera Jana Ignacego Paderewskiego do naczelnika państwa
O trzeźwość w ocenie sytuacji
input.summary: This document, dated 1962, is from a reader's corner section of a Polish-language publication, which welcomes reader correspondence while noting that submitted opinions represent personal views and not necessarily those of the editorial board. The editorial guidelines request that contributors write on one side of the paper only, leave a left margin, and write clearly. The main article, titled "On Sobriety in Assessing the Situation" by Jerzy Boleszczyk-Zakrzewski, discusses historical Polish-Russian and Polish-Ukrainian conflicts, referencing events from 1917, 1921, and 1939–1945. The author argues that conflicts along Poland's eastern borders, involving Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine, were natural consequences of ongoing bloody struggles against Moscow's expansionism and the fight for national independence.

input.title: W odpowiedzi panu K. Abramowiczowi
input.summary: In this letter published in "Ameryka-Echo," Jerzy Boleszczyc-Zakrzewski responds to criticism from P.K. Abramowicz, defending his historical arguments and objecting to what he characterizes as crude, unfounded personal attacks. He cites a 1919 resolution of the Polish Legislative Sejm during Paderewski's premiership as evidence that his historical references are legitimate, not "pseudo-historical stories" as Abramowicz claimed. Zakrzewski argues for the enduring relevance of the Jagiellonian Union model, suggesting that the states formed from the divided Jagiellonian territories cannot survive alone and that a renewed union on modern principles remains necessary. He draws a parallel between the historical Polish-Lithuanian alliance forged in 1385 against the German threat and the contemporary situation of Poland caught between German and Russian pressures after World War II. Throughout, Zakrzewski emphasizes that, as a lawyer, he maintains dignity and restraint in public discourse, unlike his opponent.

input.title: Wilno - Marszałka miłe miasto
input.summary: This article, published in the Polish-language newspaper *Dziennik Związkowy (Zgoda)* in December 1958, describes the deep connection between Polish Marshal Józef Piłsudski and the city of Vilnius (Wilno). Written by Kazimierz A. Abramowicz, President of the Association of Vilnius Enthusiasts, the piece highlights how Piłsudski's love for Vilnius was rooted not only in personal sentiment but also in his family's centuries-long ties to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The article recounts key moments in Piłsudski's life connected to Vilnius, including his schooling there, his early political activism against Tsarist rule, and his role in liberating the city from Bolshevik forces in April 1919. It also references Piłsudski's famous vow of gratitude at the Ostra Brama shrine and his insistence that Vilnius would never be surrendered, as captured in his words: "I am a stubborn Lithuanian... I will not give them Vilnius." The piece concludes with a hopeful note that Polish hands will one day light a great flame at Piłsudski's tomb when Vilnius is liberated.

input.title: Wiadomości Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej wysłane z Polski 8 lutego 1938
input.summary: Admiral Miklós Horthy, Regent of Hungary, visited Poland starting Saturday, February 5, 1938. Horthy is recognized as a national hero who saved Hungary from communism in the tragic post-war period of 1918 and has led the country's reconstruction for 15-20 years. The visit was characterized as a state visit rather than a ceremonial celebration, reflecting the deep historical ties between Hungary and Poland that date back centuries to the times of Queen Jadwiga and King Stefan Batory. Under Horthy's leadership, successive Hungarian governments have implemented important social, economic, and constitutional reforms. Poland warmly received the Hungarian Regent at Wawel Castle, symbolizing the strong relationship between the two nations.

input.title: Serwis lotniczy Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej-List nr 17
input.summary: The document describes Hungarian Regent Admiral Miklós Horthy's state visit to Poland beginning February 5, 1938. The visit highlights the centuries-old friendship between Poland and Hungary, with no historical conflicts between the neighboring nations despite their long shared border. Horthy arrived in Kraków where he was ceremonially welcomed by Polish President Mościcki at the royal Wawel Castle, laid wreaths at Marshal Piłsudski's crypt and King Stefan Batory's tomb, and stayed in restored royal apartments. During an official dinner, both leaders exchanged toasts emphasizing the deep historical bonds, shared values, and cultural similarities between their two nations.

input.title: Memoriał w sprawie słowackiej
input.summary: The Slovak nation, linguistically and ethnically distinct from the Czechs, found itself placed under Czech dominion following World War I, despite having declared an independent Slovak republic in December 1918. The document argues that Czechs have no legitimate historical, linguistic, or ethnic claim to Slovak territory, noting that the very concept of "Czecho-Slovakia" only emerged in 1918 as a product of Czech political agitation. The author highlights the close historical ties between Slovaks and Poles, appealing to Polish leaders to recognize and support the Slovak struggle for self-determination. The document further contends that the artificial Czechoslovak state, which contains a Czech minority of five million ruling over nine million people of other nationalities, poses a threat to stability in Central Europe. It calls on Poland to take an active interest in the Slovak cause, given their shared history and the dangers posed by Czech expansionism.

input.title: Rzecznik, obrońca i realizator demokracji
input.summary: The document appears to be a Polish-language biographical retrospective describing an individual's career beginning after a "Roman revolution" in 1917, when he worked as a legal consultant. He subsequently held roles as a justice for Italy and allied states in 1918, a university professor and economic affairs chairman in 1919, and escalated to president of economic affairs for all allied nations from 1920 onward. The remainder of the document repetitively lists his role as president of economic affairs for all allied states during the months of November and December for each successive year from 1920 through at least 1980, with no variation in the description.

input.title: Federacja czy inkorporacja
input.summary: This Polish-language article from January 1955, written by Tadeusz Piszkowski, examines the debate between two competing visions for Poland's eastern policy in the years 1918–1920: Józef Piłsudski's federalist concept and Roman Dmowski's incorporationist approach. Piłsudski envisioned a federation of nations — including Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine — allied with Poland, while Dmowski favored incorporating eastern territories directly under Polish dominance. The author analyzes the political and strategic strengths and weaknesses of both programs, noting that Piłsudski's federalism was ultimately too ambitious to realize, while Dmowski's realism led him to reject cooperation with neighboring nationalist movements. The article contextualizes these historical debates as still relevant to understanding Polish national identity and eastern relations.

input.title: Dwie depesze do Kasprzyckiego
input.summary: These three documents are official Polish military communications dated April 23, 1919, sent from the General Adjutancy of the Supreme Command of Polish Forces in Warsaw-Belvedere to Major Kasprzycki aboard the Head of State's train. The first document summarizes a letter from the Chief of Staff regarding military logistics, including difficulties in dispatching the second Legion division due to a shortage of uniforms, progress in organizing the third and fourth divisions, and the advance of Bolshevik forces to Proskurov. The second document appears to be a partially encrypted telegram conveying the same message, with portions of the text replaced by numerical codes. The third document transmits intelligence from Sieroszewski about a Lithuanian government delegation (Taryba) that had arrived in Warsaw from Kaunas, expressing dissatisfaction over the Polish capture of Vilnius and seeking recognition of an independent Lithuania encompassing several provinces, while refusing to travel to Vilnius for negotiations with the Commander.

input.title: Memoriał w sprawie granic wschodnich
input.summary: This memorandum, prepared by a group of Polish borderland (Kresy) politicians and intellectuals, addresses the question of Poland's eastern borders and argues that the reborn Polish Republic should be restored to its pre-partition boundaries from 1772. The authors contend that the principle of ethnographic borders, promoted by certain Polish political factions, is selectively and unfairly applied to Poland alone, as other major powers freely incorporated non-dominant ethnic groups into their territories. They argue that Belarus and Lithuania lack the social and institutional development necessary for independent statehood and therefore require Polish guidance, as Russia is deemed both undesirable and incapable of fulfilling that role. The memorandum further asserts that these eastern borderland territories are economically and geographically tied to Poland rather than Russia, sharing water systems, agricultural-industrial exchange, and cultural development. Ultimately, the document concludes that just as Poland is indispensable to these eastern lands, those lands are equally indispensable to a viable and vital Polish state.

input.title: Depesza iskrowa w sprawie porozumienia polsko-czeskiego
input.summary: On January 30, 1919, a radio telegram from London reported that the Polish-Czechoslovak border dispute had been satisfactorily resolved at the Paris Peace Conference. Polish delegate Dmowski outlined Poland's territorial claims, including lands held before the 1772 and 1790 partitions, the province and city of Poznań, Toruń, and free access to the sea through Gdańsk. Czech delegate Beneš described the background of armed clashes along the Silesian-Czech border and noted that Czechoslovakia had entered the disputed areas on January 24, 1919, despite a demarcation agreement reached in November 1918. It was proposed and accepted by both sides that the disputed areas be occupied by Allied forces, though the final status of the Silesian industrial districts remained unresolved, as Poles comprised 55% of the population but Czechoslovakia argued the coal mines were essential to its industry. An inter-Allied reconciliation committee, composed of representatives from France, Britain, and Italy, was to travel from Paris through Vienna to Warsaw to oversee further proceedings.

input.title: List i odpis listu do Komendanta
input.summary: This letter, dated April 23, 1919, was written by Wacław Sieroszewski from Warsaw to Józef Piłsudski, reporting on meetings with an official Lithuanian Taryba delegation that had arrived from Kaunas, led by Foreign Minister Dr. Šaulys, to negotiate a Polish-Lithuanian political and military alliance against the Bolsheviks. The delegation was deeply offended that Poland had captured Vilnius without informing or involving Lithuanian-Belarusian forces, and proposed that Poland recognize Lithuanian borders encompassing the Kaunas, Vilnius, Suwałki, Grodno, and parts of Minsk gubernias. Sieroszewski and Professor Kamieniecki countered with the concept of a federated Greater Lithuanian-Belarusian Republic aligned with Poland along the 1772 borders, which the delegation firmly rejected, while Šaulys repeatedly showed clear reluctance to involve Piłsudski in the negotiations. Sieroszewski worked strategically to ensure all Lithuanian matters were channeled through Piłsudski alone, advising him not to rush back to Warsaw, as the delegation's impatience worked in Poland's diplomatic favor.

input.title: Raport polityczny z Gdańska
List w sprawie Tadeusza Kościuszki
input.summary: These documents from 1919 consist of a letter from S. Bułhakówna of Siechnowicze and a military order from the Polish Podlaskie Group regarding Tadeusz Kościuszko. In her letter, Bułhakówna describes herself as a great-great-granddaughter of Kościuszko through the Estka family line and provides information about Siechnowicze as the likely birthplace and family estate of Kościuszko, noting features of the property he designed, though the estate had been burned by retreating Russian forces. She also mentions a possible distant relative named Konstanty Kościuszko but notes that most family documents and Kościuszko's personal letters were either taken by historian Korzon or destroyed in the fire. The accompanying military order, issued by General Listowski, calls on Polish soldiers who had just liberated the Kościuszko homeland to contribute funds for a monument, memorial plaque, and restoration of Kościuszko's residence at Siechnowicze, with the effort to be inaugurated in the presence of Head of State Józef Piłsudski.

input.title: Artykuł "As mulheres polonezas"
input.summary: This document is a correspondence from Poland to the Brazilian press about Polish women's political rights. It describes how Polish women were granted voting rights in November 1919 by the Council of Ministers, recognizing their historical contributions to Poland's political life, including participation in conspiracies, battles, and the defense of the resurrected Polish state. The article details the involvement of women deputies in the Polish parliament (Dieta) from 1919 onwards, highlighting their work on various legislative committees and laws concerning alcohol prohibition, labor rights, and trafficking. It notes that in the 1928 elections, 11 women served in the new Dieta, representing various political parties including national-Catholic, centrist, populist, socialist, and Ukrainian minority groups.

input.title: Wizyta Józefa Piłsudskiego we Francji
input.summary: Marshal Joseph Pilsudski, the Supreme Commander of Polish forces and Head of State, is celebrated as a great patriot, courageous soldier, and sincere friend of France during his visit to the French Republic. Born in 1867 near Vilna, he dedicated his life from an early age to the liberation of Poland, inspired by the works of the poet Mickiewicz and driven by the memory of Russia's brutal suppression of the 1863 Polish uprising. Arrested and exiled to Siberia at the age of twenty, he emerged with an indomitable strength of character that would define his lifelong struggle for Polish independence. He became a leader in the Polish Socialist Party, clandestinely publishing revolutionary materials and organizing military associations, even as he faced repeated imprisonment and persecution by Russian authorities. By August 1914, the military organizations he had built were united under his command as the Polish Legions, which resisted both Russian and German-Austrian domination in pursuit of Polish freedom.

input.title: List do Ministerstwa Spraw Wojskowych w związku z projektem ustawy sejmowej dotyczącej wojsk polskich sformowanych poza granicami kraju
input.summary: This document consists of an official response and a draft military order from August 28, 1919, related to the integration of General Haller's Polish Army, formed in France, into the main Polish armed forces. The Supreme Commander of Polish Forces states that a proposed parliamentary law is unnecessary, as a military convention already signed between the Polish and French governments established that all Polish troops formed abroad would automatically fall under Polish High Command upon crossing into Poland. A draft order addressed to General Haller praises the army he led, drawing parallels to the Polish Legions of 1797, and honors both the soldiers and their commander for voluntarily serving the Polish cause on French soil. The draft celebrates the army's return to a free and independent Poland and commends General Haller for obediently placing his forces under national command. The draft order was ultimately rejected, with a note indicating it would be replaced by an order written personally by the Supreme Commander.

input.title: Józef Piłsudski Centennial 1867-1968
input.summary: Józef Piłsudski (1867–1968) is celebrated in this commemorative publication as a transformative leader who guided Poland from over a century of captivity to independence following World War I. Born in the Vilno region steeped in the traditions of the historic Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Piłsudski was shaped by a rich legacy of freedom, tolerance, and multi-ethnic cooperation that had long distinguished Poland from its autocratic neighbors to the East. His mother, Maria, played a particularly influential role in instilling in him a deep sense of Polish patriotism, national pride, and a commitment to fighting for Poland's liberation. The document highlights how the ideals and cultural identity of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth endured through generations despite the partitions of the eighteenth century, forming the ideological foundation of Piłsudski's political and military vision. Authored by General Tadeusz Kasprzycki, a close collaborator of Piłsudski and Poland's Minister of War in 1939, the text was published by the Piłsudski Centennial Memorial Committee in New York to honor the centennial of Piłsudski's birth.

input.title: List Borysa Sawinkowa do Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: This confidential letter, dated December 29, 1921, is addressed to Marshal Apsheron of the Polesky State and describes the author's secret trip to London in October 1921. The writer met with Soviet representative Krasin, during which he argued that the "Green" peasant movement would destroy the Bolsheviks unless the right wing of the Communist Party agreed to abolish the Cheka, recognize private property, and allow free elections to the Soviets. Following this meeting, the author was contacted by Churchill's secretary Sinclair and subsequently met with Churchill, Lord Chancellor Birkenhead, and Prime Minister Lloyd George, all of whom expressed agreement with his proposed conditions for recognizing the Soviet government. The letter concludes by noting that even Krasin privately acknowledged that the Bolsheviks would likely have to reach an agreement with the "Greens," and that a future conference in London or Cannes might present these conditions as an ultimatum to the communists.

The editorial guidelines request that contributors write on one side of the paper only, leave a left margin, and write clearly. The main article, titled "On Sobriety in Assessing the Situation" by Jerzy Boleszczyk-Zakrzewski, discusses historical Polish-Russian and Polish-Ukrainian conflicts, referencing events from 1917, 1921, and 1939–1945. The author argues that conflicts along Poland's eastern borders, involving Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine, were natural consequences of ongoing bloody struggles against Moscow's expansionism and the fight for national independence.

input.title: Kalendarz im. Marszałka Józefa Piłsudskiego ułożony przez N. Lipowskiego
input.summary: This document is a Polish calendar named after Marshal Józef Piłsudski, compiled by N. Lipowski, covering 413 years from 1614 to 2027. The calendar was created to commemorate Jan Kazimierz Ginjatowicz-Rymsza, the oldest known ancestor of Marshal Piłsudski, who was born on August 6, 1614. The document includes a biographical section about N. Lipowski, a native of Nieśwież born in 1874, who was celebrated for his extraordinary photographic memory, which was studied and praised by academics and scientists across Europe and America. Professors from universities in Vilnius, Warsaw, Poznań, London, Boston, and other institutions attested to Lipowski's remarkable mnemonic abilities, particularly his visual memory. The calendar itself is presented as a testament to Lipowski's phenomenal memory and mental capabilities.

input.title: Artykuł o pomniku marszałka w Komorowie i Szkole Podchorążych
input.summary: In autumn 1999, a monument to Marshal Józef Piłsudski was unveiled in Komorowo near Ostrów Mazowiecka, restored after nearly fifty years following its destruction by communist authorities in 1950. The monument is closely tied to the history of the Infantry Officers' Cadet School (SPP), which trained future permanent officers of the Polish Army from 1923 until 1939, with roots tracing back to the Royal Military Academy founded in 1765. The school's banner, rescued during the German invasion of 1939, was transported through Hungary and Romania and eventually ended up at the Sikorski Museum in London. Each year on promotion day, cadets stood guard at the Piłsudski monument while division commanders conducted the ceremonial promotion rites, including the bestowing of officer patents and a military parade. The article also includes personal recollections from graduates of the SPP, reflecting on the rigorous selection process, character-building methods, and the bittersweet final promotion class of 1939, whose ceremony was cancelled by the outbreak of World War II.

input.title: Federacja czy inkorporacja
input.summary: This Polish-language article from January 1955, written by Tadeusz Piszkowski, examines the debate between two competing visions for Poland's eastern policy in the years 1918–1920: Józef Piłsudski's federalist concept and Roman Dmowski's incorporationist approach. Piłsudski envisioned a federation of nations — including Lithuania, Belarus, and Ukraine — allied with Poland, while Dmowski favored incorporating eastern territories directly under Polish dominance. The author analyzes the political and strategic strengths and weaknesses of both programs, noting that Piłsudski's federalism was ultimately too ambitious to realize, while Dmowski's realism led him to reject cooperation with neighboring nationalist movements. The article contextualizes these historical debates as still relevant to understanding Polish national identity and eastern relations.

input.summary: This document is a 1952 bulletin from the Secretariat of Branch Circles of a Polish exile organization in London, containing messages from General Anders and the Polish Government-in-Exile. It commemorates the August 15, 1920 Battle of Warsaw, in which Polish forces under Józef Piłsudski defeated the Bolsheviks, and draws parallels to the ongoing struggle against Soviet domination. The Polish Government-in-Exile formally protests the new constitution imposed on Poland by the communist regime in Warsaw on July 22, 1952, denouncing it as a Soviet-directed instrument that further subordinates Poland to the USSR. The bulletin also addresses the question of reconstituting Polish Armed Forces in the West, with Prime Minister General Odzierzyński emphasizing that any such effort must be based on formal treaties with Western governments to ensure that Polish sacrifices would not be in vain. Throughout the document, Polish exile leaders express hope and determination that their struggle will ultimately lead to the restoration of a free, independent, and sovereign Poland.

input.title: Centrolew, Bereza i Stronnictwo Ludowe
input.summary: This document discusses two main topics: a government housing policy and a historical-political debate about the Centrolew coalition in interwar Poland. The housing section describes a government initiative claiming to have provided new homes for over 100 million citizens, eliminated poverty, homelessness, and slums, while also developing infrastructure, education, healthcare, and other public services. The political section references an article published in "America-Echo" on December 28, 1961, by F. Skowronek, discussing the Centrolew — a pre-war (1918–1939) opposition alliance comprising the PPS, the Peasant Party, and other parties, formed to oppose the Sanacja regime after Piłsudski's 1926 coup. The coalition organized major demonstrations in Kraków in 1930, but was dissolved after the Sanacja allegedly falsified election results and arrested its leaders, imprisoning them in the Brest Fortress. The document concludes with a rebuttal directed at Skowronek, accusing him of historical inaccuracies and reminding him of his responsibilities as a Polish émigré writer.

input.title: Orędzie Prezydenta Rzeczypospolitej na dzień Święta Narodowego 3 Maja
input.summary: This document from the Polish Telegraphic Agency (PAT), dated April 23, 1955, contains several items related to the Polish government-in-exile in London. The centerpiece is a message from President August Zaleski on the occasion of the May 3rd National Holiday, in which he draws parallels between the Constitution of May 3, 1791, and the April Constitution of 1935, urging Polish emigrants to preserve the latter until Poland's liberation from foreign occupation. The document also announces the establishment of a Chapter of the Order of Polonia Restituta, listing its eight appointed members. Additionally, PAT proposes that the emigrant and Polish diaspora press conduct a reader survey on the fate of the Wawel Treasures currently stored in Canada, outlining three possible options: maintaining the current storage conditions, depositing them in a Washington museum, or returning them to Poland. The document concludes with brief notes denying rumors of government contact with Mikołajczyk's party and announcing the constitution of the Main Audit Commission of the National Treasury.

input.title: Orędzie Prezydenta Rzeczypospolitej na dzień Święta Narodowego 3 Maja
input.summary: This document is a bulletin from the Polish Telegraph Agency (PAT) dated April 23, 1955, containing several announcements from the Polish government-in-exile in London. It includes an address by President August Zaleski marking the May 3rd National Holiday, drawing parallels between the 1791 Constitution and the 1935 April Constitution as symbols of Polish statehood and resistance to occupation. The bulletin also covers the establishment of a Chapter of the Order of Polonia Restituta, a proposed survey regarding the fate of the Wawel Treasures stored in Canada, a denial of alleged contacts between the government and Mikołajczyk's party, and the composition of the National Treasury Audit Commission. Additionally, it announces a ceremonial session of the Council of the Republic of Poland to be held on May 3, 1955, at Kensington Town Hall in London.

input.title: Kserokopia Studia Claromontana 9/1988
input.summary: This document is a catalog of the archive and memorabilia of Maria and Ignacy Mościcki, the last president of the Second Polish Republic, held at Jasna Góra monastery. Mościcki died in Versoix, Switzerland in 1946, and his wife Maria preserved the surviving wartime materials for 33 years until her own death in Geneva in 1979, after which the collection was transferred to the Pauline Fathers at Jasna Góra in 1981. The archive is organized into nine sections covering documents related to Ignacy Mościcki, his family, Maria Mościcka, her family, various individuals, miscellaneous matters, decorations, personal objects, and a book collection. The collection includes a wide range of materials spanning 1897 to 1968, such as official documents, personal memoirs, political correspondence, photographs, press clippings, and the diary of Mościcki's adjutant Major Józef Hartman documenting the president's flight from Poland in September 1939.

input.title: Głosy prasy brazylijskiej w sprawie terytorialnych żądań sowieckich i stosunków polsko-sowieckich.
input.summary: This document is a Polish press note dated January 18, 1944, summarizing reactions from major Brazilian newspapers to Soviet territorial demands against Poland and the crossing of Polish borders by Soviet forces. Several prominent Rio de Janeiro newspapers, including O Globo, Diario da Noite, Correio da Manhã, and Jornal do Commercio, published articles sympathetic to Poland, emphasizing the country's enormous sacrifices during the war and condemning Soviet territorial ambitions. The Brazilian commentators argued that annexing Polish territory using methods reminiscent of Hitler's expansionism would contradict international law and the principles of sovereignty that the Allied nations claimed to be fighting for. Writers specifically challenged Soviet justifications for claiming eastern Polish territories, noting that the Ribbentrop-Molotov line resulted from an illegitimate pact and that the 1939 Soviet-organized plebiscite lacked legal validity. The Brazilian press broadly expressed the view that Poland, as the first nation to resist Nazi aggression and a continued Allied contributor, deserved full justice rather than becoming the war's greatest victim.

input.title: Zapis działalności Ministra Spraw Zagranicznych Rządu R.P. w Londynie Październik - Listopad 1944
input.summary: This document is an index of records from the Polish government-in-exile covering two key periods in late 1944: Prime Minister Mikołajczyk's second visit to Moscow (October 10–23, 1944) and subsequent London negotiations leading to his resignation. The Moscow visit documents include records of meetings with Stalin, Molotov, and Churchill, as well as multiple drafts of a proposed British agreement on the Polish question. The London period documents cover diplomatic correspondence and conversations with British and American officials, including Churchill, Eden, Cadogan, and Ambassador Harriman, as well as telegrams to Ambassador Ciechanowski in Washington. The collection concludes with records related to the political crisis surrounding Mikołajczyk's resignation and the formation of a new Polish government under Prime Minister Arciszewski.

input.title: Poufny Biuletyn Informacyjny Nr.99.
input.summary: In November 1944, U.S. Ambassador Harriman delivered a letter from President Roosevelt to Polish Prime Minister Mikołajczyk, stating that while the U.S. could not offer formal guarantees, it would not object to proposed border changes and population transfers if agreed upon by Poland, the Soviet Union, and Great Britain. Roosevelt also authorized Harriman to intervene with Stalin on Poland's behalf regarding Lwów and the oil fields, should the Polish government request it. Mikołajczyk was willing to accept this offer, but the other three coalition parties in the cabinet opposed it, fearing it would lead to Poland conceding Wilno and other territories east of the Curzon Line. Faced with this internal disagreement, Mikołajczyk resigned on November 24th, with President Kwapińśki being tasked with forming a new government. In private conversations, Mikołajczyk explained that pressure from the major powers had left him no choice but to resign, hoping a new government would have greater political flexibility.

input.title: Druga wizyta Premiera i Ministra Spraw Zagranicznych w Moskwie.
input.summary: This document is a classified Polish government report summarizing the second visit of Prime Minister Mikołajczyk, Foreign Minister Romer, and President Grabski to Moscow in October 1944. The visit was prompted by Churchill's unexpected trip to Moscow, during which he invited the Polish delegation to participate in discussions aimed at resolving Polish-Soviet disputes. During the conference on October 13th, Stalin insisted that any agreement required Polish recognition of the Curzon Line as the eastern border and acknowledgment of the Polish Committee of National Liberation (PKWN), while Churchill argued that Soviet sacrifices in the war justified these territorial demands and that Poland would receive compensation in the north and west. Mikołajczyk refused to accept the border terms, stating he lacked the authority to cede 40% of Polish territory and five million Poles, and that such a decision belonged to the Polish people. The conference concluded with Churchill proposing a compromise formula whereby Poland would provisionally accept the Curzon Line while retaining the right to appeal the matter at a future Peace Conference.

input.title: Text of Pope's address to College of Cardinals
input.summary: Pope Pius XII addressed the College of Cardinals on the feast of his patron saint, expressing deep anguish over the ongoing devastation of World War II and its toll on humanity. He made a passionate plea for Rome to be spared from becoming a theater of war, warning that anyone who raised a hand against the Eternal City would be guilty of "matricide in the eyes of the civilized world." The Pope emphasized the Church's role in defending justice and providing relief to the suffering, describing the dire conditions facing Rome's population, including widespread hunger and displacement. He drew historical parallels to past calamities that had struck Rome, arguing that the current crisis surpassed all previous hardships in scale and severity. Throughout his address, he stressed the Church's commitment to helping all people regardless of nationality or race, with the ultimate goal of restoring peace to a war-torn world.

input.title: Komunizm w Stanach Zjednoczonych.
input.summary: This document is a summary report from a Polish intelligence outpost ("Placówka Estezet") in New York, dated October 16, 1944, forwarding a synopsis of an article by American lawyer and economist Merwin K. Hart published in *Vital Speeches* on September 19, 1944. Hart's article warns of the dangers of communist infiltration in the United States, arguing that Soviet agents and revolutionary elements — many tracing back to post-1905 Russian émigré waves — have deeply penetrated American industrial, financial, and political life. He contends that despite the formal dissolution of the Comintern, the American Communist Party remains highly dangerous, with members sworn to advance Soviet power on U.S. soil. Hart also defends General Franco's Spain as a legitimate and strategically valuable partner for the United States, criticizing communist-driven media attacks against Franco and questioning why the State Department tolerates such foreign propaganda. He concludes by calling on America to curtail Soviet influence, noting that the USSR maintains thousands of diplomatic agents across North and South America while preparing postwar geopolitical positions even before the war has ended.

input.title: Biuletyn Informacyjny Sekretariatu Kół Oddziałowych
input.summary: This document is a 1952 bulletin from the Secretariat of Branch Circles of a Polish exile organization in London, containing messages from General Anders and the Polish Government-in-Exile. It commemorates the August 15, 1920 Battle of Warsaw, in which Polish forces under Józef Piłsudski defeated the Bolsheviks, and draws parallels to the ongoing struggle against Soviet domination. The Polish Government-in-Exile formally protests the new constitution imposed on Poland by the communist regime in Warsaw on July 22, 1952, denouncing it as a Soviet-directed instrument that further subordinates Poland to the USSR. The bulletin also addresses the question of reconstituting Polish Armed Forces in the West, with Prime Minister General Odzierzyński emphasizing that any such effort must be based on formal treaties with Western governments to ensure that Polish sacrifices would not be in vain. Throughout the document, Polish exile leaders express hope and determination that their struggle will ultimately lead to the restoration of a free, independent, and sovereign Poland.

input.title: Zawiadomieie o uroczystości przy Kopcu Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: On March 22, 1981, at 1:30 PM, a ceremony was held at the Kościuszko Mound (Kopiec Kościuszki) on Sowiniec, also known as the Mound of Independence, dedicated to Józef Piłsudski. During the event, veterans of the Polish Army deposited earth collected from battlefields spanning the years 1794 to 1920, as well as from Lenino (1943) and Monte Cassino (1944). This earth was described as having been soaked with the blood of Poles who fell between 1939 and 1945 in the fight for the independence and freedom of their homeland. The document appears to be a commemorative poster related to this patriotic ceremony.

input.title: Komunizm w Niemczech.
input.summary: In January 1945, a Polish intelligence officer in New York reported establishing contact with Ruth Fischer, a German-Jewish anti-Stalinist Communist, through Polish Foreign Ministry adviser Dr. M. Potulicki. Fischer was publishing a monthly periodical called "The Network" in New York and was writing a history of the German Communist Party, from which the officer obtained the third chapter covering the party's transformation between 1924 and 1929. The chapter, written in German, examines the relationship between the Russian Communist Party, the Comintern, and the KPD, including Stalin's interventions, military policy, and the forced alignment of the KPD with Soviet interests. Fischer had halted work on the book due to financial difficulties, but expressed willingness to complete the final chapter on the "Free German Movement since 1941" for approximately $300. The reporting officer requested authorization from his colonel to determine whether the intelligence division wished to commission the remaining chapter under those financial terms.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Krajowy przemysł azotowy w okresie lat 1917-1947
input.summary: This document is a bibliography and introduction to articles published in a 1958 Polish chemistry journal, covering research conducted before 1939 at the Chemical Research Institute's Division of Inorganic Industry. The bibliography lists Polish-language research papers from the 1930s on topics including magnesium production, silicate chemistry, road construction materials, alcohol dehydration, and phosphorite processing. The second article, by Stefan Pawlikowski of the Silesian University of Technology, provides a historical overview of the Polish nitrogen industry from 1917 to 1947. It discusses the founding of the METAN chemical company and journal in 1916–1917, as well as the establishment of Poland's first nitrogen compounds factory in Jaworzno, highlighting the role of Polish chemists in developing the country's chemical industry following independence.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia - zwrot od drukarza; Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes for a Polish historical text, providing details about various notable Polish political, military, and religious figures primarily from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The entries cover individuals such as economists, generals, bishops, politicians, and academics who played significant roles during key periods including World War I, the Polish-Soviet War, the interwar period, and World War II. Many of these figures were involved in Polish independence efforts, government service, and resistance activities during the German occupation. Several of the individuals noted were killed by German forces during World War II, while others survived by going into exile, primarily in London.

input.title: Biuletyn Informacyjny A.K.
input.summary: This document is an informational bulletin from the Home Army (AK) circle in the American occupation zone of Germany, published in Frankfurt in February-March 1948. The main article, written by Klaudiusz Hrabyk, invokes the legacy of Józef Piłsudski to argue that Polish political independence must be maintained, warning against becoming satellites or agents of foreign powers during the difficult postwar period. The bulletin emphasizes that former AK soldiers are particularly obligated to uphold the principle of Polish independence, as their five years of struggle represent a testament to that cause. Also included are New Year's remarks from General Bór-Komorowski and General Anders, who addressed Polish émigré organizations and called for organizational discipline and resistance to Soviet influence. The overarching theme is the duty of Poles in exile to preserve their national independence and moral-political integrity in the face of growing external pressures.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł (1869-1944)
input.summary: This document presents a biographical and bibliographic notice about Professor Kazimierz Jabłczyński (1869–1944), a prominent Polish chemist whose life's purpose was dedicated to science. Beyond his research contributions, which placed him among distinguished Polish chemists, he was deeply committed to popularizing scientific knowledge among the broader public, as reflected in his lectures across Poland and his popular publications on topics such as radioactive elements and atomic structure. He played an active role in the establishment of educational institutions, including what eventually became the Free University (Wolna Wszechnica), and contributed significantly to the development of the University of Warsaw's Chemistry building. Jabłczyński was also notable for his insistence on linguistic precision in Polish scientific writing, and his mentorship of students included rigorous correction of both content and language in their scholarly work.

input.title: Ignacy Mościcki - Autobiografia, część 11 - wycinek prawdopodobnie z Tygodnika Polskiego
input.summary: Ignacy Mościcki, while working in Fribourg, Switzerland, developed new methods for protecting high-voltage electrical networks from atmospheric overvoltages using capacitors, which he demonstrated at an electrotechnical congress with dramatic artificial lightning experiments. His presentations were so successful that he became a recognized authority in high-voltage electrical phenomena, and the Fribourg factory expanded its production based on his system, increasing its annual turnover by one million francs. Alongside this work, Mościcki was overseeing the construction of a nitric acid factory in Chippis, which in 1910 produced the world's first shipment of concentrated nitric acid derived solely from air, water, and electrical energy. He noted with frustration that a German engineer presented Mościcki's own explanations of electrical discharge phenomena in a published article without giving him credit, though Mościcki's greater grievance was the lack of consent rather than the missing attribution. Having completed his contractual obligations, Mościcki was then invited to contribute to the design of a new factory more than ten times larger, to be planned in Neuhausen.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Mieczysław Centnerszwer (1874-1944)
input.summary: Eugeniusz Berger was a Polish chemical engineer and professor who lectured at the Warsaw University of Technology before World War II and later became head of the Department of Inorganic Technology at the Łódź University of Technology in 1946. He conducted research on the production of phosphates and other chemical processes, and served as editor of the first postwar Polish Chemical Yearbook. Mieczysław Centnerszwer (1874–1944) was a Warsaw-born physical chemist who earned his doctorate at Leipzig under Wilhelm Ostwald and went on to conduct pioneering research on the properties of liquid sulfur dioxide as a non-aqueous solvent, including studies of electrolytic conductivity and phase equilibria. His collaborative work with Paul Walden on ionization in non-aqueous solvents is recognized as foundational to the rapidly developing field of non-aqueous solvent chemistry. The document draws on the journal "Przemysł Chemiczny" (Chemical Industry) from 1958 to profile these two significant figures in Polish chemistry.

input.title: Materiały dodatkowe dla Konferencji w San Francisco.
input.summary: This document is a Polish intelligence report from June 19, 1945, prepared by a post called "Estezet" in New York, providing supplementary materials for the San Francisco Conference (which established the United Nations). The report categorizes the participating delegations according to their expected political alignments, noting which countries would follow Great Britain, the United States, or the Soviet Union, and which would maintain independent positions. Two attachments are referenced: one providing personnel profiles of delegation members, and another characterizing the political and economic dependencies of participating states. The personnel profiles included in the document offer detailed biographical and political background on delegates from countries including Australia, Belgium, Canada, Chile, and China. The report was compiled for the Chief of the Intelligence Department of the Polish General Staff.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Ludwik Szperl (1879-1944)
input.summary: Ludwik Szperl (1879–1944) was a prominent Polish chemist and professor of organic chemistry at the Warsaw University of Technology, where he served twice as Dean of the Chemistry Department and as Rector from 1926 to 1928. Over a 43-year career, he taught at multiple institutions, was a founding member of the Polish Chemical Society, and contributed to various scientific and civic organizations. His research focused primarily on the reactions of sulfur and hydrogen sulfide with organic compounds, building on earlier work in the field of terpenes. A dedicated educator and friend to students, he authored a widely respected organic chemistry textbook and continued teaching clandestinely during the German occupation of Warsaw. The destruction of his laboratory and the hardships of the occupation undermined his health, and he died in Warsaw on April 29, 1944.

input.title: Opanowanie amerykańskiej Labor Party przez komunistów.
input.summary: This 1944 Polish intelligence report, filed from New York, details Communist efforts to infiltrate and take control of the American Labor Party (ALP) in New York State. It describes how Soviet military successes in Europe boosted Communist prestige in America, creating favorable conditions for their political infiltration of labor organizations, particularly those affiliated with the CIO. Labor leader John L. Lewis publicly warned against Communist influence in American unions, stating that Communist operatives were exploiting American goodwill toward the Soviet Union to advance their hidden agenda. The report explains that following the dissolution of the American Communist Party under Earl Browder's leadership in early 1944, Communists shifted tactics to infiltrate the ALP rather than build their own party, which had failed to recruit the minimum 10,000 registered members required to appear on the ballot. A key internal struggle within the ALP emerged between right-wing leaders like David Dubinsky, who rejected Communist collaboration, and left-wing leaders like Sidney Hillman, who welcomed it.

input.title: Raport na temat Carl Emil Ludwig Krepper'a.
input.summary: Carl Emil Ludwig Krepper, a German-born naturalized American citizen and former Lutheran pastor, was arrested by FBI agents on December 20, 1944, on charges of sabotage, violating censorship laws, and failing to register as a paid agent of German intelligence. He was accused of serving as a liaison for eight German spies who had landed on Long Island and in Florida, six of whom were sentenced to death. Krepper allegedly maintained contact with Walter Kappe, identified by the FBI as the director of a sabotage school in Berlin, communicating through coded correspondence with his wife in Berlin using the alias "P. Kaiser" and the password "YORKTOWN." Evidence against him included a handkerchief found on one of the saboteurs bearing his address written in invisible ink. Krepper faced up to 32 years in prison but was released on $30,000 bail pending trial.

input.title: Official english translation of Pope Pius XII's Christmas message, broadcast to world
input.summary: In his sixth wartime Christmas message, Pope Pius XII acknowledged the ongoing devastation of World War II while expressing hope that the suffering of nations would inspire a new era of international cooperation and lasting peace. He noted that citizens around the world were increasingly rejecting dictatorial power and turning toward democratic forms of government, which he viewed as a natural response to the failures that led to the war. The Pope affirmed that the Catholic Church does not oppose democracy, provided it genuinely serves the dignity and freedom of its citizens, and outlined the responsibilities of both citizens and leaders within a healthy democratic system. The message also drew attention to the Pope's praise of charitable nations, notably placing Spain and Ireland ahead of an otherwise alphabetical list, highlighting the Vatican's close ties with Francisco Franco's government.
