input.title: Wycinek z The New York Times: Text of Pope Pius' address outlining the fundamentals for effectuating peace on Earth; Spellman gets Truman message on his designation as a Cardinal
input.summary: On Christmas Eve 1945, Pope Pius XII delivered an address to the College of Cardinals reflecting on the end of World War II and calling for true, lasting peace, noting that while the fighting had ceased, the world remained in a painful "post-war period" requiring great effort to rebuild materially and morally. The Pope also announced plans for a historic consistory to bring the College of Cardinals to its full complement of seventy members for the first time in the twentieth century, in keeping with the limit established by Pope Sixtus V in 1586. Among those designated as new Cardinals was Archbishop Francis J. Spellman of New York, who received congratulations from President Truman and a personal visit from Mayor Fiorello La Guardia. Archbishop Spellman emphasized in a Christmas message that true peace could only come through a return to Christ, urging all peoples and nations to look to faith as the foundation for healing the wounds left by war.

input.title: Kserokopia Studia Claromontana 9/1988
input.summary: This document is a catalog of the archive and memorabilia of Maria and Ignacy Mościcki, the last president of the Second Polish Republic, held at Jasna Góra monastery. Mościcki died in Versoix, Switzerland in 1946, and his wife Maria preserved the surviving wartime materials for 33 years until her own death in Geneva in 1979, after which the collection was transferred to the Pauline Fathers at Jasna Góra in 1981. The archive is organized into nine sections covering documents related to Ignacy Mościcki, his family, Maria Mościcka, her family, various individuals, miscellaneous matters, decorations, personal objects, and a book collection. The collection includes a wide range of materials spanning 1897 to 1968, such as official documents, personal memoirs, political correspondence, photographs, press clippings, and the diary of Mościcki's adjutant Major Józef Hartman documenting the president's flight from Poland in September 1939.

input.title: Apel Kurii Metropolitalnej w Krakowie
input.summary: This 1984 letter from the Pastoral Department of the Kraków Metropolitan Curia was addressed to the city's parish priests, calling on them to encourage their congregations, particularly youth groups, to help with the restoration of the Kościuszko Mound (Kopiec Józefa Piłsudskiego) on Sowiniec hill. The mound, built to symbolize Polish independence and containing earth from over 3,000 battlefields and sacred sites from the years 1794–1921, had suffered significant neglect following World War II and the Nazi occupation, during which the occupiers had sought to destroy it as a symbol of Polish freedom. In 1980, a Citizens' Committee for the Care of the Piłsudski Mound was established, and in 1981 the mound was formally recognized as a National Memorial Monument and historic cultural landmark. Restoration work was carried out every dry Saturday from April to the end of November, and the letter provided practical details about transportation and tool availability. The letter emphasized that a nation wishing to preserve its identity must carefully protect its monuments of national memory and culture.

input.title: Kopiec Józefa Piłsudskiego na Sowińcu
input.summary: The Civic Committee for the Care of the Józef Piłsudski Mound was founded on June 23, 1980, in Kraków, with the goals of restoring and maintaining the mound—which contains soil from Polish battlefields and sites of martyrdom dating back to 1794—and preserving patriotic and independence traditions symbolized by the mound. Prior to the Committee's formation, the mound had fallen into severe neglect following World War II, becoming overgrown with trees and shrubs despite years of appeals by independence veterans to government authorities. Beginning in May 1980, a group of activists began physically clearing the mound, and after the Committee was formally established, restoration work continued on a regular basis. The mound was officially recognized as a National Memorial and historical monument in 1981, and additional soil from Polish battlefields and sites of martyrdom was ceremonially deposited there. Beyond restoration efforts, the Committee also organizes patriotic and religious ceremonies, collects historical archives and memorabilia, and has coordinated exhibitions honoring Marshal Piłsudski and other significant figures in Polish history.

input.title: Zawiadomieie o uroczystości przy Kopcu Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: On March 22, 1981, at 1:30 PM, a ceremony was held at the Kościuszko Mound (Kopiec Kościuszki) on Sowiniec, also known as the Mound of Independence, dedicated to Józef Piłsudski. During the event, veterans of the Polish Army deposited earth collected from battlefields spanning the years 1794 to 1920, as well as from Lenino (1943) and Monte Cassino (1944). This earth was described as having been soaked with the blood of Poles who fell between 1939 and 1945 in the fight for the independence and freedom of their homeland. The document appears to be a commemorative poster related to this patriotic ceremony.

input.title: Kopiec Niepodległości - 50 lat później
input.summary: This document, published in "Tydzień Polski" on November 14, 1987, appears to be a fragmented and partially corrupted continuation of an article about pilgrimage. It briefly mentions the historical shift in carpet weaving from handspun natural fibers to synthetic materials produced in factories. The text also references a figure named Rojda, who appeared before a United Nations Commission in London in 1946, and alludes to difficult working conditions and health concerns among workers in 1944. The latter portion of the document is largely unreadable due to extensive repetition of the same phrases, suggesting a printing or scanning error.

input.title: Historia Kopca Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: The Mound of Józef Piłsudski (Kopiec Józefa Piłsudskiego) in Kraków was built between 1934 and 1937 as a national monument honoring Marshal Piłsudski and Polish independence, following a tradition of mound-building dating back to pre-Christian times. Construction began on August 6, 1934, the twentieth anniversary of the First Cadre Company's march, and involved mass public participation, with up to 10,000 people per day contributing earth; over 3,600 soil samples from Polish battlefields and martyrdom sites were placed within it, earning it the title "Mound of Mounds." After Piłsudski's death in 1935, work accelerated and the mound was completed in 1937, standing 35 meters high with a granite stone bearing a Legionary cross at its summit. During the communist era, authorities deliberately allowed the mound to deteriorate by planting trees on its slopes, removing the granite capstone with a tank in 1953, and erasing all references to it from maps and guidebooks. Restoration efforts began in the 1980s and continued into the early 1990s, culminating in the reinstatement of the Legionary cross and the revival of public ceremonies at the site.

input.title: Komunizm w Niemczech.
input.summary: In January 1945, a Polish intelligence officer in New York reported establishing contact with Ruth Fischer, a German-Jewish anti-Stalinist Communist, through Polish Foreign Ministry adviser Dr. M. Potulicki. Fischer was publishing a monthly periodical called "The Network" in New York and was writing a history of the German Communist Party, from which the officer obtained the third chapter covering the party's transformation between 1924 and 1929. The chapter, written in German, examines the relationship between the Russian Communist Party, the Comintern, and the KPD, including Stalin's interventions, military policy, and the forced alignment of the KPD with Soviet interests. Fischer had halted work on the book due to financial difficulties, but expressed willingness to complete the final chapter on the "Free German Movement since 1941" for approximately $300. The reporting officer requested authorization from his colonel to determine whether the intelligence division wished to commission the remaining chapter under those financial terms.

input.title: Wierni i Wytrwali
input.summary: The Józef Piłsudski Institute in New York was founded on July 4, 1943, by Polish émigrés who had fled Poland during World War II, with the aim of preserving Polish national history and heritage abroad. Operating continuously from a modest beginning of one room and $30, the Institute grew to house an impressive archive including rare documents such as letters by Józef Piłsudski, operational orders from the Battle of Warsaw, and extensive records related to Polish uprisings and military history. In 1947, a London branch was established, and both institutes continue the work of the original Warsaw-based institute founded in 1923. The Institute publishes the annual journal "Niepodległość," containing memoirs, essays, and historical studies, and keeps members informed through its regularly published Bulletin. By its 50th anniversary in 1993, the Institute had become a internationally recognized center for the study of modern Polish history, with notable patrons and honorary members including Zbigniew Brzeziński and Władysław Bartoszewski.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia - zwrot od drukarza; Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes for a Polish historical text, providing details about various notable Polish political, military, and religious figures primarily from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The entries cover individuals such as economists, generals, bishops, politicians, and academics who played significant roles during key periods including World War I, the Polish-Soviet War, the interwar period, and World War II. Many of these figures were involved in Polish independence efforts, government service, and resistance activities during the German occupation. Several of the individuals noted were killed by German forces during World War II, while others survived by going into exile, primarily in London.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia (Dalszy ciąg); Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes and references from what appears to be a Polish historical publication called "Niepodległość" (Independence). The notes identify prominent Polish political, military, and academic figures from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including Jan Kanty Steczkowski, a politician and economist who served as Prime Minister, and Mariusz Zaruski, a brigadier general and pioneer of Polish skiing who died in Soviet captivity. Also referenced are academics such as Kazimierz Kling and Wacław Leśniański, both chemists specializing in petroleum technology, as well as Eligiusz Niewiadomski, a painter and art critic executed in 1923. The footnotes also point readers to related articles and documents within the same publication regarding topics such as the 1918 Austrian-Ukrainian treaty and various military orders.

input.title: Biuletyn Informacyjny A.K.
input.summary: This document is an informational bulletin from the Home Army (AK) circle in the American occupation zone of Germany, published in Frankfurt in February-March 1948. The main article, written by Klaudiusz Hrabyk, invokes the legacy of Józef Piłsudski to argue that Polish political independence must be maintained, warning against becoming satellites or agents of foreign powers during the difficult postwar period. The bulletin emphasizes that former AK soldiers are particularly obligated to uphold the principle of Polish independence, as their five years of struggle represent a testament to that cause. Also included are New Year's remarks from General Bór-Komorowski and General Anders, who addressed Polish émigré organizations and called for organizational discipline and resistance to Soviet influence. The overarching theme is the duty of Poles in exile to preserve their national independence and moral-political integrity in the face of growing external pressures.

input.title: Kopie klepsydr, zdięcia
input.summary: This correspondence consists of letters exchanged in 1997 between Zbigniew Drozdowski, a Warsaw resident and self-described independence movement activist, and Dr. Danuta J. Cisek, Director of the Józef Piłsudski Institute of America in New York. Drozdowski describes his decades-long involvement in commemorating Marshal Józef Piłsudski, including organizing a large patriotic ceremony in Warsaw in 1975 for the 40th anniversary of Piłsudski's death, and maintaining a private archive of independence-related materials that survived multiple searches by communist authorities. He offers to share his archival materials and exhibit them at the Institute, particularly in connection with the 130th anniversary of Piłsudski's birth in December 1997. Dr. Cisek responds on behalf of the Institute, thanking Drozdowski for donated materials and noting in a postscript that any payment arrangements would require board approval, while expressing hope for a potential reprint of a three-volume chronicle of Piłsudski's life.

input.title: Materiały dodatkowe dla Konferencji w San Francisco.
input.summary: This document is a Polish intelligence report from June 19, 1945, prepared by a post called "Estezet" in New York, providing supplementary materials for the San Francisco Conference (which established the United Nations). The report categorizes the participating delegations according to their expected political alignments, noting which countries would follow Great Britain, the United States, or the Soviet Union, and which would maintain independent positions. Two attachments are referenced: one providing personnel profiles of delegation members, and another characterizing the political and economic dependencies of participating states. The personnel profiles included in the document offer detailed biographical and political background on delegates from countries including Australia, Belgium, Canada, Chile, and China. The report was compiled for the Chief of the Intelligence Department of the Polish General Staff.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Stanisław Pilat i Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa
input.summary: The document commemorates the lives and scientific contributions of Stanisław Pilat (1881–1941) and Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa (1909–1945), a married couple who made lasting contributions to petroleum chemistry and refinery technology in Poland. Stanisław Pilat studied chemistry at leading European universities and spent over two decades working in the petroleum refining industry, pioneering new methods of crude oil distillation and refining, including projects realized in Mexico and across Poland. He later became a full professor at the Lwów Polytechnic, where he headed the Chair of Petroleum and Natural Gas Technology. His wife, Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa, was one of his students and collaborators who became a distinguished scientist in her own right, earning her doctorate and producing 25 publications on lubricating oils and hydrocarbon synthesis before her early death. Both died tragically — Stanisław was executed by the Germans in 1941, and Ewa died in 1945 — leaving behind a significant legacy in petroleum chemistry and petrochemical technology.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Zarys rozwoju przemysłu chemicznego w Polsce niepodległej
input.summary: This document excerpt from the Polish journal *Przemysł Chemiczny* (Chemical Industry) from 1958 covers the development of Poland's chemical industry during the Three-Year Plan (1947–1949) and the Six-Year Plan (1950–1955). It presents production data for nitrogenous and phosphorous fertilizers, as well as artificial fibers, alongside tables showing plan fulfillment percentages across various chemical industry enterprises. The text notes that significant organizational restructuring occurred during this period, including the establishment of the Ministry of Chemical Industry and the reorganization of industrial associations into central management boards. Investment policy during the Six-Year Plan shifted from building new factories to expanding and intensifying production at existing facilities, resulting in savings of approximately 3 billion złoty. Key expansions included dramatic growth in the pharmaceutical and plastics industries, with some facilities expanded up to 15-fold.

input.title: Serwis Informacyjny Ambasady RP przy Watykanie nr 28. Zgon arcybiskupa Gawliny
input.summary: Archbishop Józef Gawlina, the spiritual guardian of the Polish diaspora, died suddenly of a heart attack in Rome on September 21, 1964, at the age of 71. Born in Silesia in 1892, he had a distinguished career serving the Polish Catholic Church, including organizing Catholic Action, reorganizing the Catholic press in Poland, and serving as Military Bishop of the Polish Armed Forces during World War II. During the war, he accompanied Polish forces across multiple fronts, including a historic visit to the Soviet Union to minister to Polish soldiers released from labor camps, and later participated in the Battle of Monte Cassino. After the war, Pope Pius XII appointed him as spiritual caretaker of the entire Polish diaspora, a role in which he traveled extensively and undertook major publishing initiatives, including a monumental nine-volume work for the Polish Christian Millennium. His funeral was attended by high Vatican dignitaries, and Pope Paul VI sent a telegram of condolence through Cardinal Secretary of State Cicognani, praising Gawlina's faithful service to the Church.

input.title: Charakterystyka rządu w Lublinie
input.summary: A January 1945 article from the Yiddish newspaper *Forverts*, translated into Polish and forwarded by the "Estezet" intelligence post in New York, critically examines the composition of the Soviet-backed Lublin Provisional Government, arguing that most of its ministers were unknown figures with no significant political background in pre-war Poland. The article highlights the questionable credentials of key figures such as President Bierut, described as a Comintern operative, and notes that two of the more recognizable members, General Żymierski and Rzymowski, had been involved in past scandals involving bribery and plagiarism respectively. It further contends that the claimed coalition of four parties was a fiction, as the Socialist, Peasant, and Democratic parties continued to recognize the London-based Polish Government-in-Exile, and that only the Communist Party genuinely supported the Lublin government. The article traces the history of the Polish Communist Party from its 1893 origins through its internal factional struggles, its dissolution by Comintern order in 1937, and its ideological shifts, including its hostility to the national aspirations of Poland's minorities, including Jews. The document was transmitted through military intelligence channels in anticipation of the upcoming Roosevelt-Churchill-Stalin summit, where the Polish question was expected to be a central topic.

input.title: Raport wojskowo-prasowy z prasy argentyńskiej za czas od 1 do 15 maja 1945
input.summary: This document is a military-press report from June 1945, compiled by the "Estezet" post in New York, based on information from the "Salvador" post, covering Argentine press from May 1–15, 1945. The report analyzes both successful and failed strategic decisions during World War II, including Allied strengths such as British aircraft production, the Dunkirk evacuation, and American Lend-Lease policy, as well as Axis mistakes such as Italy's under-prepared entry into the war, Germany's invasion of Russia, and Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor. It also details Japan's military preparations for a homeland defense, including the formation of a Voluntary Defense Corps and a total mobilization decree requiring all Japanese citizens regardless of age to contribute to building fortifications. Additionally, the report covers the situation in Formosa, noting Japan's colonization of the island since 1895 and the demographic composition of its population of 6.5 million. The document was prepared for the Head of the Intelligence Division of the Supreme Command Staff.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Marian Świderek (1897-1949)
input.summary: This document is a memorial tribute to Marian Świderek (1897–1949), a Polish chemist and professor of organic chemistry at the Warsaw University of Technology. It highlights his extraordinary role as an organizer who rebuilt the Chemical Research Institute (later the Main Institute of Industrial Chemistry) from ruins in Warsaw after World War II, starting in 1945. Despite the devastation of the buildings, the lack of basic utilities, and severe shortages of equipment and personnel, Świderek managed to establish a functioning analytical laboratory and acquire necessary apparatus through expeditions to the recovered territories and a trip to the United States. The tribute emphasizes his remarkable ability to inspire and unite colleagues around a shared mission of scientific rebuilding, as well as his personal courage during the Warsaw Uprising, where he shielded coworkers from a grenade explosion with his own body. He is remembered not only as a scientist but above all as a tireless and gifted organizer whose dedication bordered on self-sacrifice.

input.title: Insygnia Królewskie
input.summary: This document concerns the investigation into Polish royal regalia (crown jewels) believed to be hidden in a church in Volodymyr-Volynskyi (Włodzimierz Wołyński). In 1920, the Military Minister Sosnkowski dispatched Professor Gembarzewski and Captain Żmigrodzki to search for the regalia based on intelligence suggesting they had been hidden there since 1794, when a Capuchin friar allegedly concealed the crowns, scepters, and other royal insignia within the monastery. The search ultimately failed to locate the treasures, prompting debate in the Parliamentary Military Commission about the credibility of the official report. Minister Sosnkowski subsequently proposed forming a commission of five to seven respected individuals to review the evidence and testimony, while keeping sensitive details secret so as not to hinder future searches. Correspondence was exchanged between the Minister, the President of Ministers, the Marshal of the Sejm, Bishop Dubowski, and other officials to address lingering doubts about how the investigation was conducted.

input.title: W obronie marszałka - Józef Piłsudski według prof. Zbigniewa Wójcika
input.summary: Professor Zbigniew Wójcik, who had a personal connection to Józef Piłsudski as the son of a gendarme who served the Marshal, has written a short biographical sketch titled "Józef Piłsudski 1867–1935" as a defense against what he considers slanderous attacks on Piłsudski's legacy. The book addresses common criticisms of Piłsudski, including his association with socialism, his cooperation with German and Austro-Hungarian forces, his collaboration with foreign intelligence, and accusations of treason during the 1920 Battle of Warsaw, arguing that these actions were justified by the overriding goal of Polish independence. Wójcik also defends the May Coup of 1926, rejecting the characterization of it as a "crime" by drawing comparisons to other historical leaders who seized power by force, while acknowledging that Piłsudski's treatment of political opponents in his later years was difficult to fully justify. Despite these criticisms, Wójcik concludes that Piłsudski's flaws cannot overshadow his monumental contributions as the primary architect of the restored Polish state and the leader who achieved Poland's greatest military victory since 1683.

input.title: Kopia autobiografii ś.p. Prezydenta I. Mościckiego-Rozdział XI
input.summary: The document reflects on Polish history, particularly the internal weaknesses of pre-partition Poland, including the excessive privileges of the nobility, lack of civic development, and the inability of cities and rural populations to counterbalance these failures. It describes how these vulnerabilities allowed neighboring powers to partition Poland three times between 1772 and 1795, extinguishing Polish statehood. During the long period of foreign occupation, Polish society channeled its energy into repeated uprisings and resistance movements rather than constructive state-building. Despite this, a strong idealistic and patriotic spirit, reinforced by religious sentiment especially among the rural majority, helped preserve national identity and unity across the three partitions. The author contrasts this Polish idealism with Switzerland, where he observed that practical civic virtues rather than idealism had been sufficient to build a well-functioning and cultured state.

input.title: Informacje dotyczące rodziny Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: This document is a compilation of genealogical and heraldic references to the Piłsudski (Piłsudzki) family, gathered by Szymon Kowarski from various Polish noble family registers and heraldic publications from the late 18th and 19th centuries. The sources document numerous marriages between members of the Piłsudski family and other noble families of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, particularly in the Żmudź (Samogitia) region. Several members of the family held notable offices, including Antoni Piłsudzki as sword-bearer of Żmudź, Franciszek and Ignacy Piłsudzki as Lithuanian cupbearers, and Stanisław Piłsudzki as marshal of the Rosień district. The records also note property holdings and inheritances associated with the family, such as the Billewicze estate passing to the Piłsudskis and Anna Ciołkowska née Piłsudzka bequeathing 100,000 złoty for poor students in her 1853 testament.

input.title: Artykuł "As mulheres polonezas"
input.summary: This document is a correspondence from Poland to the Brazilian press about Polish women's political rights. It describes how Polish women were granted voting rights in November 1919 by the Council of Ministers, recognizing their historical contributions to Poland's political life, including participation in conspiracies, battles, and the defense of the resurrected Polish state. The article details the involvement of women deputies in the Polish parliament (Dieta) from 1919 onwards, highlighting their work on various legislative committees and laws concerning alcohol prohibition, labor rights, and trafficking. It notes that in the 1928 elections, 11 women served in the new Dieta, representing various political parties including national-Catholic, centrist, populist, socialist, and Ukrainian minority groups.

input.title: Kopiec Józefa Piłsudskiego na Sowińcu
input.summary: The Civic Committee for the Care of the Józef Piłsudski Mound was founded on June 23, 1980, in Kraków, with the goals of restoring and maintaining the mound—which contains soil from Polish battlefields and sites of martyrdom dating back to 1794—and preserving patriotic and independence traditions symbolized by the mound. Prior to the Committee's formation, the mound had fallen into severe neglect following World War II, becoming overgrown with trees and shrubs despite years of appeals by independence veterans to government authorities. Beginning in May 1980, a group of activists began physically clearing the mound, and after the Committee was formally established, restoration work continued on a regular basis. The mound was officially recognized as a National Memorial and historical monument in 1981, and additional soil from Polish battlefields and sites of martyrdom was ceremonially deposited there. Beyond restoration efforts, the Committee also organizes patriotic and religious ceremonies, collects historical archives and memorabilia, and has coordinated exhibitions honoring Marshal Piłsudski and other significant figures in Polish history.

input.title: Obiad w Sulejówku
input.summary: This document is from a February 1, 1930 edition of the Polish newspaper *Dzień Polski* and contains a personal account by Mikołaj Sokolnicki about Marshal Józef Piłsudski. In the first section, Sokolnicki recalls sitting beside Piłsudski during the Sejm deliberations in Riga, describing the Marshal's calm voice, patriotic passion, and a moving speech calling for national unity to build a strong, independent Poland. The second section appears to be a more fragmented, emotionally charged narrative depicting an intense personal encounter with the Commander, conveying his visible pain and strong feelings. The repeated phrases suggest either a printing error or a stylistic device emphasizing the dramatic weight of the moment. Overall, the document reflects a tone of deep admiration and reverence for Piłsudski as a national leader.

input.title: Artykuły z New York Times'a dotyczące sytuacji w Polsce
input.summary: The British House of Commons passed the coal bill on its third and final reading following a turbulent all-night debate, during which Labor members Jack Jones and J. H. Thomas were ejected and suspended respectively for defying the Speaker's authority. Prime Minister Baldwin praised the bill as a satisfactory measure that would resolve the ongoing coal dispute, with his government defeating a Labor amendment to reject it by a majority of 222 votes. However, miners who had been on strike for nine weeks rejected the bill, arguing it would impose wage reductions and longer working hours. Separately, League of Nations financial commissioners Jeremiah Smith and Royall Tyler completed their missions in Austria and Hungary, having successfully reorganized the finances of both nations since 1922 and 1924 respectively. Additionally, a new school for nurses was announced in Warsaw, Poland, with the American Red Cross supporting the adoption of an American nursing program.

input.title: Gdy Wielkopolanie gościli Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: This document, written by Stefan Stablewski in Kraków in July 1967 to commemorate the centenary of Józef Piłsudski's birth, recounts the Polish Head of State's three-day visit to the Wielkopolska region in July 1921. During the visit, Piłsudski participated in military exercises near Nakło on the Noteć River and was entertained at the estate of Konstanty Bniński in Samostrzel, where he was hosted by local nobility including the Chłapowski, Jezierski, and Deszczorowski families. The visit culminated at Kórnik Castle, where Piłsudski was welcomed by the Brotherhood of Marksmen and met with the distinguished Zamoyski family, who had previously sheltered him during his years as a political émigré. Stablewski reflects on the historical significance of the meeting between Piłsudski and Władysław Zamoyski, noting their shared devotion to Polish independence despite their differing political temperaments and approaches.

input.title: Józef Piłsudski Centennial 1867-1968
input.summary: Józef Piłsudski (1867–1968) is celebrated in this commemorative publication as a transformative leader who guided Poland from over a century of captivity to independence following World War I. Born in the Vilno region steeped in the traditions of the historic Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Piłsudski was shaped by a rich legacy of freedom, tolerance, and multi-ethnic cooperation that had long distinguished Poland from its autocratic neighbors to the East. His mother, Maria, played a particularly influential role in instilling in him a deep sense of Polish patriotism, national pride, and a commitment to fighting for Poland's liberation. The document highlights how the ideals and cultural identity of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth endured through generations despite the partitions of the eighteenth century, forming the ideological foundation of Piłsudski's political and military vision. Authored by General Tadeusz Kasprzycki, a close collaborator of Piłsudski and Poland's Minister of War in 1939, the text was published by the Piłsudski Centennial Memorial Committee in New York to honor the centennial of Piłsudski's birth.

input.title: Rozkaz na dzień 12 maja 1938
input.summary: This document is a Polish-language publication from May 12, 1938, commemorating the third anniversary of the death of Marshal Józef Piłsudski, the founder of modern Poland. It includes an official order from the leadership of the Strzelec (Riflemen's Association) calling on members to draw strength and inspiration from Piłsudski's legacy and to remain committed to his ideals of Polish greatness and independence. The document also features a poem honoring Piłsudski's burial sites at Wawel and Rossa, as well as reflective prose urging every Polish citizen to examine their conscience and renew their dedication to serving Poland. Additionally, it briefly notes celebrations of the May 3rd Constitution anniversary in Warsaw, where approximately 15,000 members of military and social organizations, including 4,000 from the Riflemen's Association, gathered in tribute. Throughout, the overarching theme is one of national duty, remembrance, and unwavering loyalty to Piłsudski's vision of a powerful, independent Poland.

input.title: Serwis lotniczy Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej- fragmenty listu nr 6
input.summary: This Polish intelligence document from December 31, 1937 reports on several domestic and international incidents. It describes an assault on a Polish postman and military chaplain in Gdańsk by a Free City official named Neubauer, who received only a fine. The document also reports on Soviet authorities' forcible deportation of residents from the town of Dyasan near Poland's border, accused of pro-Polish sympathies, with their homes taken over by border guards. Additional items cover Polish industrial production growth, Prince Michał Radziwiłł's engagement in Nice, a Paris city council decision to name a street after Marshal Piłsudski, and the sentencing of communist Ukrainian separatists in Tarnopol.

input.title: Wiadomości Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej wysłane z Polski 25 stycznia 1938
input.summary: This Polish document from January 31, 1938, reports on several topics: the development of Poland's war industry under General Litwinowicz, who explained how Marshal Piłsudski ordered the creation of military industry in the center of the state, and how Poland had to rebuild from having almost no weapons production facilities after the partitions. It describes the opening of a new youth center for the World Association of Poles from Abroad in Gronik near Zakopane. The document also includes extensive testimonies from veterans of the 1863 January Uprising, including 90-year-old fighters recounting their experiences, and concludes with General Wieniawa-Długoszowski laying a wreath at Romuald Traugutt's execution site and Marshal Śmigły-Rydz decorating the veterans with medals.

input.title: Serwis lotniczy Polskiej Agencji Telegraficznej- List nr 13
input.summary: This document from January 25, 1938 commemorates the 75th anniversary of the January Uprising of 1863 against Russian rule. Marshal Piłsudski viewed 1863 as a pivotal moment when old Poland died and new Poland was born, with this uprising serving as a spiritual precursor to Poland's armed struggle for independence in 1914. The article describes ceremonies in Warsaw where President Mościcki received 54 surviving veterans (50 men and 4 women) at the Royal Castle, and includes their personal accounts of battles, wounds, and hardships endured during the uprising. The celebrations emphasized the continuity between the 1863 insurgents and modern Poland's independence, with Marshal Śmigły-Rydz honoring the veterans and connecting their sacrifice to the legacy of both Romuald Traugutt (the uprising's martyred leader) and Marshal Piłsudski.

input.title: Uroczystości pogrzebowe w stolicy
input.summary: This May 15, 1935 edition of the *Dziennik Związkowy* (Polish Daily Zgoda) reports on the death and upcoming funeral of Marshal Józef Piłsudski, the founder of modern Poland. His body was lying in state at the Belweder Palace in Warsaw, with an urn containing his heart, his military decorations, baton, and cap placed on the catafalque, along with an image of the Virgin Mary of the Gate of Dawn to whom he was especially devoted. The funeral ceremonies were scheduled for Friday in Warsaw, with his coffin to be interred alongside the royal tombs at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków on Saturday. The paper also notes that the newly appointed Inspector of the Polish Armed Forces, Rydz-Śmigły, issued a statement outlining his military career, and that the official press and Polish organizations both at home and abroad called for national unity in mourning Piłsudski's passing.

input.title: Gdy Wódz odchodził w wieczność
input.summary: This document is a commemorative album in Polish documenting the state funeral ceremonies for Marshal Józef Piłsudski, the First Marshal of Poland, who died on May 12, 1935, at 8:45 PM in the Belweder Palace in Warsaw. The album follows the funeral procession from the Belweder Palace through the streets of Warsaw, including a stop at St. John's Cathedral, and then to Mokotów Field, before the journey to Kraków. The procession was attended by Polish military generals, government officials, the President of the Republic, Piłsudski's family, and foreign dignitaries including representatives from France, Germany, Romania, and other nations. The album includes photographs and descriptions of the ornate funeral arrangements, such as the casket carried on a gun carriage drawn by six black horses, accompanied by Piłsudski's personal sword, baton, and cap, with his heart preserved separately in an urn. The document serves as a solemn tribute to a leader described as having given everything to Poland while asking nothing for himself.

input.title: Kopia autobiografii ś.p. Prezydenta I. Mościckiego-Rozdział I
input.summary: Ignacy Mościcki was born on December 1, 1867, in Mierzanowo, in the Płock region of Poland, into a family with a strong patriotic tradition, as both his father and grandfather participated in Polish uprisings against Russian rule. During his early schooling in Zamość, he actively resisted Russian cultural oppression, refusing to attend Orthodox church services and defying bans on speaking Polish, which led him to transfer to a private school in Warsaw. At the Warsaw secondary school, he excelled in mathematics and natural sciences but struggled with subjects requiring memorization, a gap he believed later affected his ability to express himself in writing and in foreign languages. From an early age, Mościcki demonstrated strong independence and self-discipline, imposing strict personal regimens on himself to build character, including attempting to sleep on bare wooden boards to toughen his resolve. His upbringing, marked by physical vigor, personal freedom, and early responsibility, played a significant role in shaping his character and sense of personal dignity.

input.title: Maszynopis autobiografi Prezydenta Ignacego Mościckiego-Rozdział I
input.summary: The narrator was born in 1867 in Mierzanowo, Poland, into a landowning family with a strong patriotic tradition, as both his father and grandfather participated in Polish uprisings against Russian rule. He described himself as a sensitive but self-controlled child who was raised with great freedom and independence, which fostered a strong sense of personal responsibility from an early age. During his schooling in Zamość, he actively resisted Russian cultural oppression, refusing to attend Orthodox church services and ignoring bans on speaking Polish, which eventually led him to transfer to a private school in Warsaw. In Warsaw, he excelled in mathematics and the natural sciences but struggled with rote memorization, a weakness he compensated for by developing strong analytical and spatial reasoning skills. He also subjected himself to rigorous self-discipline throughout his school years, deliberately imposing hardships on himself to strengthen his character, though not always with successful results.

input.title: Ignacy Mościcki - Autobiografia, część 1 - wycinek prawdopodobnie z Tygodnika Polskiego
input.summary: Ignacy Mościcki (1867–1946) is widely known as a historical figure primarily due to his 13 years as President of Poland, though historians generally regard him as a mediocre politician. Less recognized is his remarkable career as a scientist, inventor, and industrial organizer, whose practical discoveries brought him international renown and significant wealth, transforming him from a London barber's assistant into a celebrated chemist. His autobiography reveals two distinct sides of his character, with the sections on his scientific work being far more vivid and compelling than those on his political life. Born into a patriotic landed family with a strong tradition of involvement in Polish uprisings, Mościcki describes a childhood marked by physical vigor, intellectual independence, and early resistance to Russian oppression in his school years. From a young age, he cultivated self-discipline and a talent for analytical thinking over rote memorization, traits that would later prove decisive in his scientific achievements.

input.title: Komentarz do Protokólarnego Spisu Inwentarza Gabinetu Służbowego Józefa Piłsudskiego Pierwszego Marszałka Polski
input.summary: This document is a commentary on the inventory of the official office of Józef Piłsudski, the First Marshal of Poland, located in the building of the General Inspector of the Armed Forces in Warsaw. It describes a major renovation carried out in 1933 while Piłsudski was on vacation, which included repainting, new furnishings, installation of a bathroom, an elevator, and updated electrical lighting, all overseen by Colonel Wartha. The document also notes Piłsudski's conservative nature regarding changes to his surroundings and his mixed reactions upon returning to the renovated office. Additional improvements were made in 1934, including the installation of a mountain air purification system invented by President Mościcki and a small kitchen. The second part of the commentary provides detailed notes on individual inventory items, including their origins, manufacturers, and purposes.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Metan
input.summary: In 1916, the METAN Company was founded in Lwów with the goal of conducting scientific research into natural gas and developing rational methods for its utilization, at a time when the natural gas industry in the region was highly primitive and wasteful. Led by Professor Ignacy Mościcki and Dr. Kazimierz Kling, the organization functioned essentially as a chemical research institute, funding itself through the sale of patents and licenses. Shortly after its founding, METAN also launched a professional journal of the same name, which published pioneering works on natural gas, petroleum, and related chemical industries. By 1920, the scope of the institute's work had broadened significantly beyond natural gas to encompass coal processing and general chemical industry topics, prompting the journal to be renamed *Przemysł Chemiczny* (Chemical Industry). The article credits METAN's work and its members, particularly engineers Wieleżyński and Szaynok, with contributing meaningfully to the development of Poland's natural gas and chemical industries in the years following World War I.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia (Dalszy ciąg); Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes and references from what appears to be a Polish historical publication called "Niepodległość" (Independence). The notes identify prominent Polish political, military, and academic figures from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including Jan Kanty Steczkowski, a politician and economist who served as Prime Minister, and Mariusz Zaruski, a brigadier general and pioneer of Polish skiing who died in Soviet captivity. Also referenced are academics such as Kazimierz Kling and Wacław Leśniański, both chemists specializing in petroleum technology, as well as Eligiusz Niewiadomski, a painter and art critic executed in 1923. The footnotes also point readers to related articles and documents within the same publication regarding topics such as the 1918 Austrian-Ukrainian treaty and various military orders.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Ludwik Szperl (1879-1944)
input.summary: Ludwik Szperl (1879–1944) was a prominent Polish chemist and professor of organic chemistry at the Warsaw University of Technology, where he served twice as Dean of the Chemistry Department and as Rector from 1926 to 1928. Over a 43-year career, he taught at multiple institutions, was a founding member of the Polish Chemical Society, and contributed to various scientific and civic organizations. His research focused primarily on the reactions of sulfur and hydrogen sulfide with organic compounds, building on earlier work in the field of terpenes. A dedicated educator and friend to students, he authored a widely respected organic chemistry textbook and continued teaching clandestinely during the German occupation of Warsaw. The destruction of his laboratory and the hardships of the occupation undermined his health, and he died in Warsaw on April 29, 1944.

input.title: Opanowanie amerykańskiej Labor Party przez komunistów.
input.summary: This 1944 Polish intelligence report, filed from New York, details Communist efforts to infiltrate and take control of the American Labor Party (ALP) in New York State. It describes how Soviet military successes in Europe boosted Communist prestige in America, creating favorable conditions for their political infiltration of labor organizations, particularly those affiliated with the CIO. Labor leader John L. Lewis publicly warned against Communist influence in American unions, stating that Communist operatives were exploiting American goodwill toward the Soviet Union to advance their hidden agenda. The report explains that following the dissolution of the American Communist Party under Earl Browder's leadership in early 1944, Communists shifted tactics to infiltrate the ALP rather than build their own party, which had failed to recruit the minimum 10,000 registered members required to appear on the ballot. A key internal struggle within the ALP emerged between right-wing leaders like David Dubinsky, who rejected Communist collaboration, and left-wing leaders like Sidney Hillman, who welcomed it.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Stanisław Pilat i Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa
input.summary: The document commemorates the lives and scientific contributions of Stanisław Pilat (1881–1941) and Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa (1909–1945), a married couple who made lasting contributions to petroleum chemistry and refinery technology in Poland. Stanisław Pilat studied chemistry at leading European universities and spent over two decades working in the petroleum refining industry, pioneering new methods of crude oil distillation and refining, including projects realized in Mexico and across Poland. He later became a full professor at the Lwów Polytechnic, where he headed the Chair of Petroleum and Natural Gas Technology. His wife, Ewa Neyman-Pilatowa, was one of his students and collaborators who became a distinguished scientist in her own right, earning her doctorate and producing 25 publications on lubricating oils and hydrocarbon synthesis before her early death. Both died tragically — Stanisław was executed by the Germans in 1941, and Ewa died in 1945 — leaving behind a significant legacy in petroleum chemistry and petrochemical technology.

input.title: Raport na temat Carl Emil Ludwig Krepper'a.
input.summary: Carl Emil Ludwig Krepper, a German-born naturalized American citizen and former Lutheran pastor, was arrested by FBI agents on December 20, 1944, on charges of sabotage, violating censorship laws, and failing to register as a paid agent of German intelligence. He was accused of serving as a liaison for eight German spies who had landed on Long Island and in Florida, six of whom were sentenced to death. Krepper allegedly maintained contact with Walter Kappe, identified by the FBI as the director of a sabotage school in Berlin, communicating through coded correspondence with his wife in Berlin using the alias "P. Kaiser" and the password "YORKTOWN." Evidence against him included a handkerchief found on one of the saboteurs bearing his address written in invisible ink. Krepper faced up to 32 years in prison but was released on $30,000 bail pending trial.

input.title: Karta ewidencyjna - Józef Adwent
input.summary: This document is a military registration card ("Karta Ewidencyjna") for Józef Adwent, a Polish lieutenant born on March 19, 1886, in the village of Oględów in the Kielce region. Before Polish independence, he served in the Russian Army's artillery from 1907, participating in World War I on the Austrian, Carpathian, and Romanian fronts, where he was wounded twice and decorated with five military honors, including the Cross of St. George. He joined the Polish Army on April 4, 1919, serving under General Żeligowski's division in Odessa, and by February 1920 had risen to battery commander in the 1st Lithuanian-Belarusian Field Artillery Regiment. His commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Jan Górski, assessed him as a very good, diligent, and well-trained artillerist who was fully suited for the role of battery commander.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Walenty Dominik (1891-1944)
input.summary: Prof. Walenty Dominik (1891–1944) was born in Dobczyce, Poland, and overcame significant financial hardship to complete his chemical engineering studies at the Lwów Polytechnic in 1914, earning his doctorate in 1917. He worked in various industrial roles, including as chief chemist at the AZOT factory in Jaworzno, before taking up a professorship in chemistry at the Warsaw University of Life Sciences (SGGW) in 1923, where he taught for twenty years. His research encompassed chemical technology, wood technology, and agricultural chemistry, and he was recognized with the Gold Cross of Merit in 1936 and elected a corresponding member of the Warsaw Scientific Society. Among his notable practical contributions was the development of a fuel mixture based primarily on crude alcohol with a small addition of technical ether, aimed at reducing Poland's dependence on imported gasoline as motorization grew.

input.title: Die Unabhängigkeitsbestrebungen der Polen
input.summary: This document, archived at the Piłsudski Institute in New York, is a classified 1913 report by Austro-Hungarian General Staff Captain Josef Rybak detailing Polish independence movements. It traces the history of Polish independence efforts from the partitions through various socialist and nationalist parties, particularly the PPS (Polish Socialist Party) and its alliances with other left-wing organizations. The report describes how the failed 1905 revolution prompted the PPS to shift toward systematic military organization and preparation for a future armed uprising. It also covers a significant August 1912 conference in Zakopane, where representatives of multiple Polish independence-oriented parties passed resolutions committing to pursue Polish independence and oppose any accommodation with the partitioning powers. The document reflects Austrian intelligence monitoring of Polish political and paramilitary activities in the years leading up to World War I.

input.title: PPS a niepodległość Polski
input.summary: At the outbreak of World War I in August 1914, the Polish workers' movement was deeply fragmented, divided among several competing factions including the PPS Revolutionary Fraction, PPS Opposition, PPS Left, and the SDKPiL, each holding differing positions on the war and Polish independence. These divisions mirrored broader splits within Polish society, with some groups supporting Piłsudski's legionary movement against tsarism while others held pro-Russian sympathies or anti-war stances in line with the Second International's 1910 resolutions. The ideological conflicts within the PPS had been building since 1905, when disagreements over revolutionary tactics and the independence question caused significant internal tensions, ultimately leading to a party split in 1906. The PPS Left eventually removed the goal of Polish independence from its program, while the PPS Revolutionary Fraction, under Piłsudski's influence, moved away from Marxism toward an emphasis on armed combat organizations. The shared goal of independence ultimately led the PPS Revolutionary Fraction and PPS Opposition to reunite under the PPS banner.

input.title: Życie i czyny Marszałka
input.summary: Józef Piłsudski was a Polish statesman and military leader who dedicated his life to the cause of Polish independence, enduring Siberian exile, imprisonment in a Warsaw citadel, and internment in Magdeburg by the Germans. He organized secret publications, military associations, and ultimately the Polish Legions, which began marching against Russian forces in August 1914. After being released from German imprisonment in November 1918, he returned to Warsaw and assumed leadership of the newly reborn Polish state, successfully repelling a Bolshevik invasion that threatened Warsaw in August 1920. Following a period of political withdrawal in the early 1920s, he staged a military intervention in May 1926 to restore order to a chaotic parliamentary system, thereafter serving as Minister of Military Affairs and twice as Prime Minister. Throughout his life, Piłsudski remained a man of simple personal needs, and his legacy of patriotism and sacrifice for the Polish nation is remembered as an enduring lesson for future generations.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Józef Szczęsny Turski (1883-1955)
input.summary: In 1945, Professor Świderek undertook the enormous task of rebuilding the Chemical Research Institute in Warsaw from ruins, as the buildings had been stripped of equipment and used as SS storage facilities during the occupation, with no water, electricity, or gas supply. Despite these desperate conditions, he established an analytical laboratory that same year, organized expeditions to recover equipment from the recovered territories, and personally recruited pre-war chemists to join the effort. In 1947, he traveled to the United States to purchase scientific apparatus and books, and he also established a branch of the Institute in Gliwice to better serve Poland's chemical industry centers. Known for his exceptional organizational abilities and dedication, Świderek worked tirelessly—often until midnight—driven by a profound belief in the importance of Polish chemistry. The document also briefly introduces Professor Józef Szczęsny Turski (1883–1955), a globally recognized authority in dye chemistry who independently discovered the direct amination of aromatic compounds and made significant contributions to anthraquinone chemistry despite a life marked by hardship and historical upheaval.

input.title: Sprawa zaangażowania Adama Bobrowskiego i Kamili Choma-Iberszerowej.
input.summary: This document consists of secret Polish military intelligence correspondence from Manchester dated July 31, 1943, requesting the engagement of two civilian employees for the Independent Intelligence Post in Manchester, Canada, beginning September 1, 1943. The first candidate, Adam Bobrowski, is recommended as a civilian referent at a salary of $160 USD per month, based on his prior intelligence cooperation, knowledge of Canadian affairs, and proficiency in English, French, German, and Ukrainian. The second candidate, Kamila Choma-Iberszerowa, is recommended as a civilian typist-clerk at $120 USD per month, praised for her discretion, organizational skills, and exemplary conduct. The author requests a telegraphic decision from headquarters in London, as Bobrowski requires three weeks' notice to leave his current position with Canadian Censorship. Accompanying the letters are the résumés and photographs of both candidates, along with detailed justifications for their appointments.

input.title: Notatka do Konsulatu RP w Amsterdamie
input.summary: This document, dated January 20, 1940, is an official communication from the Consular Division of the Polish Legation in Stockholm to the Polish Consulate in Amsterdam. It warns relevant humanitarian institutions about three Polish citizens: Kazimierz Konecki (real surname Kon), journalist, born November 18, 1909; Józef Lichtensztul, lawyer, born June 6, 1906; and Roman Szmuler, private clerk, born January 23, 1905, all born in Warsaw. The three individuals had already received tickets to travel to Paris from the Jewish Committee in Kaunas, but nonetheless fraudulently obtained additional travel funds and living expenses from the local Jewish community in Stockholm. Konecki and Lichtensztul also received financial assistance from the Polish Relief Committee under false pretenses. Copies of the document were sent to the Polish Legation in The Hague, the Polish Consulate in Brussels, and the Polish Consulate General in Paris.

input.title: Die "P. P. S." Organisationsdaten
input.summary: This document is a 1913 report from the General Staff of the Austro-Hungarian k.u.k. I Corps providing organizational details about the Polish Socialist Party (P.P.S.). It describes the party's leadership structure, which consists of four main committees: the Central Workers' Committee (C.K.R.), the Organizational Committee, the Combat Committee, and the Foreign Committee. The C.K.R., based in Warsaw, directed activities related to preparing for a Polish revolution, including arms acquisition and independence propaganda, and operated a central school training revolutionaries in military subjects such as tactics, explosives, and intelligence. The party was active throughout Russian Poland, Lithuania, and Ukraine, with additional members in Russian universities and influence within the Russian Army itself. The Combat Committee (Wydzial Bojowy) further supported revolutionary efforts by publishing military training pamphlets covering topics such as weapons handling, demolition, and tactics for distribution among the proletariat.

input.title: Prośba do Konsulatu R.P. o sporządzenie tłumaczenia na język portugalski świadectw urodzenia i chrztu
input.summary: This document from the Polish Consulate in Rio de Janeiro, dated September 1920, records a request by Kazimierz Reychman for translation and legalization of birth and baptism certificates for his two sons. The certificates concern João Antonio Venceslau Reychman, born February 19, 1910, and Estevão Adolpho Reychman, born June 28, 1908, both in Warsaw. The documents include both their original Evangelical-Reformed birth and baptism records, as well as certificates showing their acceptance into the Roman Catholic Church in December 1917. The Polish Consulate provided official Portuguese translations of these documents from the original Polish versions.

input.title: List Piłsudskiego do Jodko-Narkiewicza
input.summary: Written in Kraków on February 21, 1909, this letter from "Ziuk" to Jodka-Narkiewicz discusses the author's recovering health, noting he has been taking short walks but tires easily. He requests that the recipient visit him by February 28th at the latest so they can discuss and coordinate their positions in detail before an upcoming conference on March 3rd in Vienna. The writer plans to leave Kraków on March 1st to arrive in Vienna a day early to rest before the conference, as instructed by his doctor. He also mentions writing to "Władek" asking him to come directly to Vienna on the 3rd, emphasizing it is necessary for him to be fully informed of all discussions. The letter closes with greetings from the author's wife to both the recipient and his companion.

input.title: List Piłsudskiego zapewne do Jodko-Narkiewicza
input.summary: This document is a letter written by Józef Piłsudski (signed "Ziuk") from Kraków around January 11-12, 1909, inviting his close friend Jedko-Narkiewicz to meet on Sunday. Piłsudski outlines three reasons for the meeting: a mysterious proposal from "the East" (a codename for Japan) requiring a quick response, a desire to discuss his role and boundaries within the party among trusted friends, and further discussion of "evening matters." He expresses concern about potential ideological differences with his colleagues and fears that his continued course of action might lead to conflict with them. The meeting referenced in the editorial notes was a gathering where Piłsudski discussed his plans for creating a military organization (the Union of Active Struggle), which faced opposition from some party members.

input.title: List Piłsudskiego
input.summary: This document contains a letter written by "Ziuk" (likely Józef Piłsudski) in early June 1909, addressed to an unnamed close friend. The letter discusses the matter of a person named Witold, urging the recipient to visit someone referred to as "pan I." regarding Witold's affairs, as Ignacy had written about the situation. The writer also mentions returning soon with "Agr." (Agrafka), identified in the notes as Władysław Dehnel, a member of the Polish Socialist Party (PPS) involved in smuggling underground publications and weapons. Additionally, Ziuk briefly mentions having prepared a list of articles but feels no motivation to write about any matters. The accompanying notes provide biographical details about Dehnel and clarify the Russian phrase "oczistki sowiesti," meaning "for a clear conscience."

input.title: List Piłsudskiego z Abbazii
input.summary: Written in Abbazia on February 27, 1909, this letter from Ziuk informs the recipient that he has already sent a telegram asking Stefan to come visit him immediately, but then reconsidered, worried they might miss each other en route. He explains that his schedule depends on an upcoming conference date, which can be confirmed through Władek, and that he plans to leave for Vienna two days before the conference. He instructs that if Stefan arrives in Abbazia after he has already departed, Stefan should be redirected to Vienna to meet Jowisz or Gustaw. The letter closes with a brief mention that snow has fallen for two days, that his health treatment has been somewhat hampered by the warm and fresh air, though he is improving, and sends greetings from both himself and his family.
