input.title: Komunikat informacyjny nr 3.
input.summary: This document is an informational communiqué (No. 3) dated February 7, 1931, issued by the Second Department of the Polish General Staff in Warsaw, concerning the situation in Soviet Ukraine. The report covers a wide range of topics, including Soviet Ukrainian administration, national minority affairs, Communist Party activities, labor and social welfare issues, education and culture, and economic matters such as agriculture, industry, electrification, transportation, and finance. The document also includes a section on the question of Ukrainian independence, featuring reviews of pro-Polish Ukrainian emigrant press, opposition and hostile press, foreign press coverage, and a bibliography. The sources utilized include Soviet newspapers, Russian émigré press, and Ukrainian émigré publications from late 1930 and early 1931.

input.title: Komunikat informacyjny nr 5.
input.summary: This document is an informational bulletin (Kommunikat Informacyjny No. 5) dated March 31, 1931, produced by the Second Department (Intelligence) of the Polish General Staff, focusing on the situation in Soviet Ukraine. It covers a wide range of topics including anti-Polish agitation, the relationship between the population and the Soviet state, Communist Party affairs, nationality issues (particularly Ukrainization policies), military matters, education and culture, and economic conditions. The bulletin also includes a review of Ukrainian press publications, both those sympathetic to Poland and those in opposition, as well as émigré press from both Ukrainian and Russian sources. The document draws on a variety of Soviet press sources, including "Proletarska Prawda" and "Komunist," among others.

input.title: Pismo przewodnie do Ministerstwa Spraw Zagranicznych dotyczące wysyłki wycinków z prasy Ekwadoru wraz z załącznikami
input.summary: The Polish Embassy in Brazil forwarded press clippings from Ecuador dated May-June 1929 to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Warsaw. The main article from "Diario del Pueblo" reports that Poland, with a population of 30 million and facing emigration pressures, aspires to obtain colonial territories in Central Africa. The article states that Poland, along with Germany, Italy, and Japan, plans to request colonial mandates when the League of Nations reviews the colonial distributions from 1919 at its 1929 session. Poland claims the right to demand a portion of former German colonies, specifically seeking approximately 100,000 square kilometers in Central Africa.

input.title: Centrolew, Bereza i Stronnictwo Ludowe
input.summary: This document discusses two main topics: a government housing policy and a historical-political debate about the Centrolew coalition in interwar Poland. The housing section describes a government initiative claiming to have provided new homes for over 100 million citizens, eliminated poverty, homelessness, and slums, while also developing infrastructure, education, healthcare, and other public services. The political section references an article published in "America-Echo" on December 28, 1961, by F. Skowronek, discussing the Centrolew — a pre-war (1918–1939) opposition alliance comprising the PPS, the Peasant Party, and other parties, formed to oppose the Sanacja regime after Piłsudski's 1926 coup. The coalition organized major demonstrations in Kraków in 1930, but was dissolved after the Sanacja allegedly falsified election results and arrested its leaders, imprisoning them in the Brest Fortress. The document concludes with a rebuttal directed at Skowronek, accusing him of historical inaccuracies and reminding him of his responsibilities as a Polish émigré writer.

input.title: Komunizm w Niemczech.
input.summary: In January 1945, a Polish intelligence officer in New York reported establishing contact with Ruth Fischer, a German-Jewish anti-Stalinist Communist, through Polish Foreign Ministry adviser Dr. M. Potulicki. Fischer was publishing a monthly periodical called "The Network" in New York and was writing a history of the German Communist Party, from which the officer obtained the third chapter covering the party's transformation between 1924 and 1929. The chapter, written in German, examines the relationship between the Russian Communist Party, the Comintern, and the KPD, including Stalin's interventions, military policy, and the forced alignment of the KPD with Soviet interests. Fischer had halted work on the book due to financial difficulties, but expressed willingness to complete the final chapter on the "Free German Movement since 1941" for approximately $300. The reporting officer requested authorization from his colonel to determine whether the intelligence division wished to commission the remaining chapter under those financial terms.

input.title: List o odnalezieniu nowego mazurka Fryderyka Chopina
input.summary: This document from the Polish Legation in Rio de Janeiro (1931) discusses the recent discovery of a previously unknown Chopin mazurka in A-flat major. The manuscript, written in Chopin's own hand and dated "Paris 1834," was found in a musical album that originally belonged to Polish pianist Maria Szymanowska and later passed to the family of poet Adam Mickiewicz. The mazurka, though from Chopin's juvenile period, displays characteristic features of his mature works and was likely given to the Mickiewicz family either by Chopin himself or after his death in 1849. The album was donated to the Adam Mickiewicz Museum in Paris by Maria Mickiewicz, the poet's granddaughter.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Krajowy przemysł azotowy w okresie lat 1917-1947
input.summary: This document is a bibliography and introduction to articles published in a 1958 Polish chemistry journal, covering research conducted before 1939 at the Chemical Research Institute's Division of Inorganic Industry. The bibliography lists Polish-language research papers from the 1930s on topics including magnesium production, silicate chemistry, road construction materials, alcohol dehydration, and phosphorite processing. The second article, by Stefan Pawlikowski of the Silesian University of Technology, provides a historical overview of the Polish nitrogen industry from 1917 to 1947. It discusses the founding of the METAN chemical company and journal in 1916–1917, as well as the establishment of Poland's first nitrogen compounds factory in Jaworzno, highlighting the role of Polish chemists in developing the country's chemical industry following independence.

input.title: Komentarz do Protokólarnego Spisu Inwentarza Gabinetu Służbowego Józefa Piłsudskiego Pierwszego Marszałka Polski
input.summary: This document is a commentary on the inventory of the official office of Józef Piłsudski, the First Marshal of Poland, located in the building of the General Inspector of the Armed Forces in Warsaw. It describes a major renovation carried out in 1933 while Piłsudski was on vacation, which included repainting, new furnishings, installation of a bathroom, an elevator, and updated electrical lighting, all overseen by Colonel Wartha. The document also notes Piłsudski's conservative nature regarding changes to his surroundings and his mixed reactions upon returning to the renovated office. Additional improvements were made in 1934, including the installation of a mountain air purification system invented by President Mościcki and a small kitchen. The second part of the commentary provides detailed notes on individual inventory items, including their origins, manufacturers, and purposes.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia - zwrot od drukarza; Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes for a Polish historical text, providing details about various notable Polish political, military, and religious figures primarily from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The entries cover individuals such as economists, generals, bishops, politicians, and academics who played significant roles during key periods including World War I, the Polish-Soviet War, the interwar period, and World War II. Many of these figures were involved in Polish independence efforts, government service, and resistance activities during the German occupation. Several of the individuals noted were killed by German forces during World War II, while others survived by going into exile, primarily in London.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Jan Zawidzki (1866-1928)
input.summary: Jan Zawidzki (1866–1928) was a prominent Polish chemist who studied at the Riga Polytechnic and later at the University of Leipzig under Wilhelm Ostwald, where he earned his doctorate. His doctoral dissertation, in which he experimentally verified the Duhem-Margules equation by measuring vapor pressures of liquid mixtures, is considered a classic contribution to the study of phase equilibria. During his professorships in Dublany and later at the Warsaw Polytechnic, he focused primarily on chemical kinetics, particularly developing a systematic classification of autocatalytic reactions that is regarded as a culmination of classical kinetics. Zawidzki also made significant contributions to the history of Polish chemistry and left behind an extensive two-volume inorganic chemistry textbook, published posthumously, which was the only original academic-level inorganic chemistry text in Polish before World War II. Beyond his scientific work, he played an important organizational role in Polish higher education, serving as rector of the Warsaw Polytechnic during the difficult period of 1918–1920.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł (1869-1944)
input.summary: This document presents a biographical and bibliographic notice about Professor Kazimierz Jabłczyński (1869–1944), a prominent Polish chemist whose life's purpose was dedicated to science. Beyond his research contributions, which placed him among distinguished Polish chemists, he was deeply committed to popularizing scientific knowledge among the broader public, as reflected in his lectures across Poland and his popular publications on topics such as radioactive elements and atomic structure. He played an active role in the establishment of educational institutions, including what eventually became the Free University (Wolna Wszechnica), and contributed significantly to the development of the University of Warsaw's Chemistry building. Jabłczyński was also notable for his insistence on linguistic precision in Polish scientific writing, and his mentorship of students included rigorous correction of both content and language in their scholarly work.

input.title: Ignacy Mościcki - Autobiografia, część 10 - wycinek prawdopodobnie z Tygodnika Polskiego
input.summary: Ignacy Mościcki, a Polish scientist working in Switzerland, developed an innovative method for producing nitric acid using rotating electric flame furnaces, achieving nitrogen oxide concentrations two and a half times higher than his Norwegian competitor Birkeland. His work attracted the attention of the Swiss company "Aluminium Industrie A.G. Neuhausen," leading to a signed agreement in 1908 that provided him with 250,000 francs and a monthly salary of 2,000 francs in exchange for designing, building, and operating a nitric acid factory in Chippis. He also invented new absorption towers with ten times the efficiency of existing designs, a breakthrough that remained unrivaled for over thirty years and was patented across Europe. During this period, Mościcki maintained close ties with the Polish community in Freiburg, hosting students in his home and financially supporting Polish youth studying abroad. He was also visited several times by Józef Piłsudski, who brought associates including Aleksander Prystor, a future Polish prime minister.

input.title: Karta ewidencyjna Anatola Piłsudskiego
input.summary: Anatol Piłsudski, born in 1874 in Russia, was a Polish Roman Catholic musician and diplomat who trained at the Imperial Conservatory in St. Petersburg and held prominent musical positions in Irkutsk and Kishinev before the upheavals of the early 20th century displaced him. After working in a railway office in Murmansk and briefly seeking employment in Lithuania and Poland, he emigrated to Brazil, where he worked as a music teacher and piano repairman in Rio de Janeiro from 1924 to 1928. From 1929 to 1931, he served as librarian and archivist at the Polish Legation in Rio de Janeiro, having been taken on largely due to his distinguished surname and his reputation as a cultured and knowledgeable musician. His personnel evaluation describes him as diligent, intelligent, energetic, and tactful, though noting that his poor health, artistic temperament, and monarchist inclinations made him less suited to bureaucratic work. He was married to a Russian woman, Helena née Diegtińska, and they had two children.

input.title: Materiały dodatkowe dla Konferencji w San Francisco.
input.summary: This document is a Polish intelligence report from June 19, 1945, prepared by a post called "Estezet" in New York, providing supplementary materials for the San Francisco Conference (which established the United Nations). The report categorizes the participating delegations according to their expected political alignments, noting which countries would follow Great Britain, the United States, or the Soviet Union, and which would maintain independent positions. Two attachments are referenced: one providing personnel profiles of delegation members, and another characterizing the political and economic dependencies of participating states. The personnel profiles included in the document offer detailed biographical and political background on delegates from countries including Australia, Belgium, Canada, Chile, and China. The report was compiled for the Chief of the Intelligence Department of the Polish General Staff.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Michał Chorąży (1904-1948)
input.summary: Dr. Michał Chorąży (1904–1948) was a prominent Polish chemist specializing in coal chemistry and technology, who began his research career in 1927 at the Chemical Research Institute in Warsaw under Professor Świętosławski. He earned his doctorate in 1931 from the Warsaw University of Technology and gained international experience working in Professor Wheeler's laboratory in Sheffield, England. From 1935 to 1939, he served as director of the Walenty coking plant in Ruda Śląska, where he conducted successful technical experiments on improving coke quality, while also lecturing at the Warsaw University of Technology. During the German occupation, he refused to collaborate with the occupiers and worked instead in private Polish peat extraction. After the war, he played a pivotal role in rebuilding Poland's coking industry in Silesia, organizing research institutions and resuming scientific work until his death in 1948.

input.title: Raport Kongresowej Komisji Dies'a dotyczący działalności Komitetu politycznej akcji CIO
input.summary: The document is a report from the "ESTEZET" intelligence post in New York, dated May 16, 1944, submitted to Polish military intelligence. It summarizes the findings of the U.S. Congressional Dies Committee's report on the political activities of the CIO's (Congress of Industrial Organizations) Political Action Committee. The Dies Committee's 215-page report accused the CIO's Political Action Committee of being a front for communist activity, alleging that known communists had taken control of key positions within the organization and that its leader, Sidney Hillman, was operating under the direction of American Communist Party chief Earl Browder. In response, Hillman vehemently denied the accusations and attacked Dies as a liar, arguing that the committee's investigation was a politically motivated attempt to undermine the American labor movement ahead of the 1944 presidential election. The document also notes that Dies himself was a controversial and widely criticized figure, viewed by liberals, labor leaders, and Roosevelt allies as a demagogue and ultra-nationalist whose tactics were compared by Vice President Henry Wallace to those of Nazi propagandist Goebbels.

input.title: Opinie inspektorskie za 1936 dowódców pułków, brygad, grup, piech. dyw. i dyw. piech - stan z dnia 01.02.1937r.
input.summary: This document consists of Polish military inspection reports from 1936, evaluating the performance and suitability of various infantry colonels and lieutenant colonels for command positions. The assessments cover each officer's service history, including their roles in World War I and the Polish-Bolshevik War, as well as their peacetime command experience. Evaluations range from highly favorable, such as Colonel Kustroń being described as an outstanding officer fully suited for division command, to more critical assessments, such as Colonel Piwnicki being rated as average due to lacking energy and sound tactical judgment. Several officers are noted as well-prepared for regimental or divisional command, while others are recommended for staff roles better suited to their skills. The reports reflect a systematic effort to assess battlefield readiness and leadership potential within the Polish Army officer corps.

input.title: Odezwa do wszystkic byłych członków  K.O.N.
input.summary: This document is an appeal from the Detroit District Historical Commission of the National Defense Committee (K.O.N.) to all former members of the organization regarding the publication of a history of the K.O.N. Following a district conference held on March 22nd at the Polish House, a commission was established and an appeal for cooperation was sent to progressive publications and active members across America. The commission is inviting all former K.O.N. members and supporters of the independence movement from 1914–1920 to attend a follow-up conference on May 17th at the People's Hall at Harper and Jos. Campau streets. The appeal calls on members to unite their efforts to preserve and pass on to future generations the significant work of the National Defense Committee, invoking their traditional motto of civic duty, solidarity, and action.

input.title: Kopia autobiografii ś.p. Prezydenta I. Mościckiego-Rozdział XX
input.summary: Poland's state budget in the interwar period was extremely limited at around 2 billion zlotys, which proved insufficient to meet the country's urgent needs, particularly military rearmament. The author recounts his repeated but unsuccessful efforts to appoint the more capable Kwiatkowski as Finance Minister, facing resistance from Piłsudski and his inner circle, while a series of less effective ministers — Matuszewski, Jan Piłsudski, and Zawadzki — led the ministry with poor results over many years. Only in 1935 was Kwiatkowski finally appointed, exceeding all expectations, though by then the author deeply regretted that six years had been lost. The document reflects on Poland's broader economic weaknesses, including a largely rural and poor population, underdeveloped financial institutions, and limited domestic capital accumulation, which together constrained the country's economic and military development. The author expresses a haunting belief that more capable economic management throughout the 1920s and 1930s might have prevented the catastrophe of 1939.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia - zwrot od drukarza; Rozdział XX
input.summary: The document discusses Poland's financial challenges during the late 1920s and early 1930s, focusing on the selection and performance of successive Ministers of Finance. The author recounts recommending Kwiatkowski for the finance ministry to Piłsudski in 1929, but being rejected due to distrust within Piłsudski's inner circle, leading instead to a series of inadequate ministers — Matuszewski, Jan Piłsudski, and Zawadzki — whose conservative or ineffective policies worsened the country's financial state during the economic crisis. It was not until 1935 that Kwiatkowski was finally appointed, exceeding all expectations, though the author laments that six wasted years may have contributed to Poland's catastrophe in 1939. The document also reflects on Poland's broader economic struggles, including a low savings rate, an underdeveloped rural economy, and limited capital available for long-term investment, all of which constrained the state's ability to fund critical needs such as military rearmament.

input.title: Biuletyn Informacyjny Sekretariatu Kół Oddziałowych
input.summary: This document is a 1952 bulletin from the Secretariat of Branch Circles of a Polish exile organization in London, containing messages from General Anders and the Polish Government-in-Exile. It commemorates the August 15, 1920 Battle of Warsaw, in which Polish forces under Józef Piłsudski defeated the Bolsheviks, and draws parallels to the ongoing struggle against Soviet domination. The Polish Government-in-Exile formally protests the new constitution imposed on Poland by the communist regime in Warsaw on July 22, 1952, denouncing it as a Soviet-directed instrument that further subordinates Poland to the USSR. The bulletin also addresses the question of reconstituting Polish Armed Forces in the West, with Prime Minister General Odzierzyński emphasizing that any such effort must be based on formal treaties with Western governments to ensure that Polish sacrifices would not be in vain. Throughout the document, Polish exile leaders express hope and determination that their struggle will ultimately lead to the restoration of a free, independent, and sovereign Poland.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Krajowy przemysł azotowy w okresie lat 1917-1947
input.summary: This document is a bibliography and introduction to articles published in a 1958 Polish chemistry journal, covering research conducted before 1939 at the Chemical Research Institute's Division of Inorganic Industry. The bibliography lists Polish-language research papers from the 1930s on topics including magnesium production, silicate chemistry, road construction materials, alcohol dehydration, and phosphorite processing. The second article, by Stefan Pawlikowski of the Silesian University of Technology, provides a historical overview of the Polish nitrogen industry from 1917 to 1947. It discusses the founding of the METAN chemical company and journal in 1916–1917, as well as the establishment of Poland's first nitrogen compounds factory in Jaworzno, highlighting the role of Polish chemists in developing the country's chemical industry following independence.

input.title: Wspomnienia i relacje Ignacy Mościcki Autobiografia - zwrot od drukarza; Przypisy
input.summary: This document consists of biographical footnotes for a Polish historical text, providing details about various notable Polish political, military, and religious figures primarily from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The entries cover individuals such as economists, generals, bishops, politicians, and academics who played significant roles during key periods including World War I, the Polish-Soviet War, the interwar period, and World War II. Many of these figures were involved in Polish independence efforts, government service, and resistance activities during the German occupation. Several of the individuals noted were killed by German forces during World War II, while others survived by going into exile, primarily in London.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Józef Szczęsny Turski (1883-1955)
input.summary: In 1945, Professor Świderek undertook the enormous task of rebuilding the Chemical Research Institute in Warsaw from ruins, as the buildings had been stripped of equipment and used as SS storage facilities during the occupation, with no water, electricity, or gas supply. Despite these desperate conditions, he established an analytical laboratory that same year, organized expeditions to recover equipment from the recovered territories, and personally recruited pre-war chemists to join the effort. In 1947, he traveled to the United States to purchase scientific apparatus and books, and he also established a branch of the Institute in Gliwice to better serve Poland's chemical industry centers. Known for his exceptional organizational abilities and dedication, Świderek worked tirelessly—often until midnight—driven by a profound belief in the importance of Polish chemistry. The document also briefly introduces Professor Józef Szczęsny Turski (1883–1955), a globally recognized authority in dye chemistry who independently discovered the direct amination of aromatic compounds and made significant contributions to anthraquinone chemistry despite a life marked by hardship and historical upheaval.

input.title: Przemysł Chemiczny Tom 37 nr 4/1958-artykuł Józef Zawadzki (1886-1951)
input.summary: This document is a transcription of articles from the 1958 Polish journal "Przemysł Chemiczny" (Chemical Industry), profiling two notable Polish scientists. The first section describes the work of Professor J. S. Turski, who conducted extensive research on rapeseed oil, organizing his work into five thematic groups covering topics such as agrotechnical issues, refining processes, and the industrial use of erucic acid for producing alcohols, amines, and surfactants. The second section honors Professor Józef Zawadzki (1886–1951), a prominent figure in Polish chemical science and engineering education who played a key role in shaping the Chemical Faculty at the Warsaw University of Technology and championing the importance of physical chemistry in chemical technology. Zawadzki was also instrumental in establishing the Polish Academy of Technical Sciences, participated in the Polish Chemical Society, and during the German occupation helped organize clandestine higher education and postwar academic planning. Both profiles highlight scientists who made lasting contributions to Polish chemistry and technical education despite significant personal and historical hardships.

input.title: Przemówienie Mieczysława Sokołowskiego na posiedzeniu Rady Narodowej.
input.summary: In a speech delivered to the National Council on March 9, 1951, Polish Foreign Minister Mieczysław Sokołowski analyzed the shifting global balance of power, noting that the Soviet Union had strengthened its position through the acquisition of atomic technology and the communist conquest of China, while Western powers had begun serious rearmament efforts. He argued that the Korean War demonstrated that the USSR had significantly increased its tolerance for military risk in its offensive actions, even without directly seeking full-scale open war — a posture he compared to the legal concept of "dolus eventualis." Sokołowski contended that while the Soviets continued to prefer cold war tactics, including internal subversion and exploiting divisions within the West, the danger of the cold war escalating into open armed conflict had grown considerably. Despite acknowledging ongoing disagreements among Western powers on issues such as Communist China and Formosa, he expressed confidence that the rearmament drive and the growing Atlantic alliance would ultimately strengthen the free world's defensive position. He concluded with a cautionary note that the Western powers had not yet fully shed their appeasement-era tendencies, and that a truly active policy in defense of freedom for all nations remained a distant but necessary goal.

input.title: Przemówienie Mieczysława Sokołowskiego na posiedzeniu Rady Narodowej
input.summary: In a speech delivered to the National Council on March 9, 1951, Polish Foreign Minister Mieczysław Sokołowski analyzed the global balance of power, identifying two key factors shaping the international conflict: the Soviet Union's acquisition of atomic technology and its expanded influence in the Far East following the communist conquest of China, alongside Western nations' renewed rearmament efforts. He argued that the Korean War represented an unambiguous act of communist aggression, and that the USSR's handling of the conflict — particularly its allowance of Chinese communist intervention — signaled a significant and dangerous shift in Soviet foreign policy. Sokołowski assessed that while the Soviets were not yet seeking large-scale open warfare, they had substantially increased their tolerance for the risk of such a conflict, comparable to the legal concept of "dolus eventualis," meaning they pursued aggressive actions while accepting the possibility of war as a potential consequence. Despite noting divisions within the Western camp and some appeasement tendencies, he expressed confidence that the rearmament of Western nations and the strengthening of the Atlantic alliance would ultimately prove decisive. He urged steadfast loyalty to the Western bloc, believing that as its strength grew, its policies would become increasingly effective.

input.title: Biuletyn Informacyjny Sekretariatu Kół Oddziałowych
input.summary: This document is a bulletin from a Polish military organization, dated July-August 1951, commemorating August 15th as Polish Soldier's Day, which marks the anniversary of the 1920 Battle of Warsaw. The bulletin includes a message from General Anders urging Polish soldiers to remain vigilant and prepared to fight for Poland's independence against communist tyranny. The document provides a detailed account of the 1920 Polish-Soviet War, highlighting how Marshal Józef Piłsudski led a unified Polish nation to a decisive victory over the Soviet Red Army, saving not only Poland but also Western Europe from Soviet domination. The text notes that this victory was achieved without Western assistance, and in fact despite interference, drawing a parallel to the later betrayal of Poland at Yalta and Tehran. The bulletin concludes with the lesson that Poland's freedom must be won through its own efforts and sacrifice, as no one will grant it as a gift.

input.title: 5 posiedzenie Rady Narodowej R.P.
input.summary: At the 5th session of the 2nd sitting of the Polish National Council, held on April 13, 1951, in London, the Council approved the state budget for the period from April 1, 1951 to March 31, 1952. The session, chaired by Vice-Chairman Stanisław Mackiewicz, began with a tribute to the recently deceased Ambassador Juliusz Łukasiewicz. During the budget debate, several representatives raised concerns about the budget being too high relative to available resources, noting that only approximately 45% of the budget had secured funding, with roughly 30% covered by the National Treasury. While most political clubs ultimately voted in favor of the budget, some members abstained, and speakers urged the government to exercise caution and restraint in its expenditures. Additional political matters were also discussed, including concerns about Polish exiles being recruited into foreign armies, the dangers of atomic warfare, and the need to strengthen Polish independence efforts abroad.

input.title: Sprawozdanie prezesa Rady Ministrów
input.summary: This document is an excerpt from the diary of the Polish National Council, dated October 17, 1953, containing a report by Prime Minister General Dr. R. Odzierzyński. The report focuses primarily on the Communist regime's intensifying persecution of the Catholic Church in Poland, culminating in the imprisonment of Cardinal Wyszyński, the Polish Primate. The speaker outlines a systematic campaign against religious institutions, including the annulment of the concordat, removal of religious education from schools, liquidation of Catholic charities and monasteries, arrest of priests and bishops, and the staging of show trials, most notably that of Bishop Kaczmarek. The Prime Minister emphasizes that these actions are part of a long-term Kremlin-directed strategy to eradicate spiritual and religious life in Poland, and that any apparent softening of the campaign is merely tactical. The Polish government-in-exile expresses solidarity with the Church and the Polish people, while refraining from judging the difficult decisions made by the clergy operating under occupation.

input.title: Odczyty, przemówienia i artykuły ambasadora  Józefa Lipskiego w języku polskim i angielskim
input.summary: This document consists of two parts: a note concerning the Polish-German liquidation agreement of October 31, 1929, and a historical analysis of the decisive period in Polish-German relations leading up to World War II. The 1929 liquidation agreement resolved mutual financial claims stemming from World War I and the Treaty of Versailles, with both governments mutually renouncing claims on behalf of themselves and their citizens, and Poland agreeing to cease liquidation of German property on its territory. The second section examines how Nazi Germany sought to draw Poland into a military alliance directed against the Soviet Union, offering territorial incentives including influence over Soviet territories, but Poland consistently refused these overtures in order to maintain its balanced foreign policy toward both powerful neighbors. Germany's expansionist ideology of "Lebensraum" in the East was a core tenet of National Socialism, and Poland's refusal to cooperate with these plans is identified as a fundamental underlying cause of Hitler's decision to destroy the Polish state in September 1939. The document notes that various Nazi leaders, including Goering and Ribbentrop, pursued these initiatives through competing channels of diplomacy, with Goering specifically tasked with overseeing Polish-German relations during the period of 1935–1938.

input.title: Pismo M. Sokołowskiego do rządów mocarstw zachodnich.
input.summary: Polish Foreign Minister M. Sokołowski sent a letter to the governments of the United States, Great Britain, and France in connection with a planned Council of Four Foreign Ministers meeting. He argued that the goal of securing lasting peace could not be achieved without ending the unlawful Soviet occupation of Poland and other Central-Eastern European countries, which had extended Soviet control over more than 120 million people and destabilized European political and economic balance. Sokołowski warned that the occupied nations could become both victims and instruments of further Soviet expansionist ambitions, and that the Soviet western border of 1939 represented the furthest line at which Europe could resist Communist Russian imperialism. He pledged that once liberated, Poland would actively participate in international cooperation under its legitimate democratic government. Additionally, on March 5, 1951, the President of the Polish Republic appointed seven new members to the Polish National Council.

input.title: Pismo M. Sokołowskiego do rządów mocarstw zachodnich.
input.summary: Polish Foreign Minister M. Sokołowski sent a letter to the governments of the United States, Great Britain, and France in connection with a proposed meeting of the Council of Four Foreign Ministers. In the letter, he argued that the goal of lasting peace cannot be achieved without ending the unlawful Soviet occupation of Poland and other Central and Eastern European countries, which has extended Soviet control over more than 120 million people. He contended that this occupation has destroyed the foundations of European political and economic balance and serves as a stepping stone for further conquests. Sokołowski emphasized that the Soviet western border of 1939 represented the furthest line at which Europe could resist Communist Russian imperialism, and that ending the Soviet occupation is therefore a vital interest of all free nations. The document also notes that on March 5, 1951, the President of the Polish Republic appointed seven new members to the Polish National Council.

input.title: List ugrupowań politycznych do gen. Mariana Kukieły.
input.summary: Written in London on August 21, 1951, this letter from three Polish political organizations in exile — the Liga Niepodległości Polski, Stronnictwo Ludowe "Wolność," and Stronnictwo Pracy — is addressed to General Marian Kukiel and reaffirms their positions on three key points of a proposed political agreement. The signatories express support for the formation of a genuine National Council of the Republic of Poland (Rada Narodowa R.P.) composed of representatives chosen by political and social organizations, with authority to oversee the government's budget and political activities. They also agree to the President of the Republic convening consultative meetings with political leaders, while firmly opposing any arrangement that would reduce the President's constitutional role to merely rubber-stamping decisions made by an informal committee. The organizations urge that a meeting of the six political groups be convened before September 4, 1951 to resolve the question of forming the National Council, and indicate their willingness to continue negotiations even if full agreement is not reached before the Council's first session.

input.title: List T. Bieleckiego do gen. Kukiela
input.summary: Written on 26 November 1951 from London, this letter from T. Bielecki to a General summarizes the failure of four months of negotiations aimed at unifying Polish political forces in exile. Bielecki outlines a comprehensive proposal he submitted on 23 October covering the powers of the President and the formation of a National Unity Council, but complains that after two weeks without response, the reply he received on 6 November fundamentally reversed the agreed positions rather than offering modest modifications. The core dispute centers on whether the President should exercise his personal prerogatives without accountability or be bound by a democratic advisory majority of party representatives. Additional unresolved issues include the President's relationship to the National Unity Council, the duration of his term, and whether the Council should be formed organically or through presidential decree. Given these unresolved fundamental disagreements, Bielecki concludes that convening a six-party conference would be premature until the President clearly defines his stance on limiting his own powers.

input.title: 7 posiedzenie Rady Narodowej R.P.
input.summary: The 7th session of the Polish National Council (Rada Narodowa R.P.) was held on May 18, 1951, under the chairmanship of Vice-Chairman Jerzy Kuncewicz, during which Professor Józef Poniatowski was announced as the new Council member replacing the late Ambassador Juliusz Łukasiewicz. The Prime Minister responded to an interpellation regarding consultations on the nomination of a presidential successor, noting that the process had been unsuccessful as three political parties outside the Council refused to provide substantive responses, though the government expressed hope for eventual agreement. The Council also received and referred to the Budget-Treasury Commission two audit reports on the National Treasury, both of which confirmed that the accounting had been conducted properly and that expenditures were maintained within reasonable limits. Additionally, the Legal Commission's report on the so-called Paris Agreement was unanimously adopted, declaring that President's 1939 Paris statement on personal powers was a political act rather than a legal norm. Finally, the Military Commission presented a resolution on rebuilding Polish Armed Forces in the West, emphasizing that restoring Polish independence through armed effort was the supreme goal, and opposing the conscription of Polish citizens into foreign armies while seeking Allied recognition of Polish freedom as a war objective.

input.title: Przemówienie ministra dla Spraw Obywateli Polskich na Obczyźnie
input.summary: In a 1951 speech to the National Council, Polish Minister Zygmunt Rusinek presented the government's proposed decrees regarding the structure and membership of the Fourth National Council in exile. He argued against a competing proposal from the Independent Social Group, contending that the government's version better ensured continuous, independent public oversight of the government by establishing clear limits on gaps between Council terms and minimum membership requirements. Rusinek emphasized the government's commitment to eventually holding general elections among Polish exiles abroad, while acknowledging ongoing disputes that made immediate elections impractical. The proposed decree outlined that nine-tenths of Council members would be nominated independently of the government, with political parties representing the independence movement providing half of all nominations, in order to ensure the Council's broad representativeness and independence.

input.title: List T. Bieleckiego do gen. Kukiela
input.summary: Written from London on November 12, 1951, this letter from T. Bielecki to a General describes the breakdown of months-long negotiations aimed at unifying Polish political forces in exile. The writer outlines a comprehensive compromise proposal submitted on October 23rd regarding the powers of the President and the formation of a National Unity Council, but states that the response received on November 8th fundamentally reversed the agreed-upon principles. The central dispute concerns whether the President should exercise his powers with the counsel of party representatives or retain unchecked personal prerogatives, with Bielecki arguing that democratic principles require the former. Additional disagreements arose over the method of forming the National Unity Council, particularly whether it should be established by decree or organically, and how its membership should be proportionally composed. Given the failure to resolve these fundamental issues after four months of difficult negotiations, Bielecki concludes that convening a six-party conference would be premature until the President clearly defines his position on limiting his personal prerogatives.

input.title: Sytuacja w Z.S.R.R. po śmierci Stalina
input.summary: Joseph Stalin suffered a stroke on the night of March 1-2, 1953, and died on March 5 at 9:50 PM in his Kremlin residence, with news of his illness having been withheld from the public until March 4. The document assesses Stalin's historical legacy, acknowledging that while official Soviet tributes overstated his role, he was nonetheless a skilled political tactician and organizer who successfully consolidated power after Lenin's death, carried out agricultural collectivization, and significantly expanded Soviet industrial capacity. Stalin remained active in the final year of his life, publishing a major work on socialist economics and addressing the 19th Congress of the Communist Party in October 1952, where he outlined plans for advancing toward full communism and pledged continued global revolutionary struggle. Following Stalin's death, Georgi Malenkov swiftly assumed full power, apparently having prepared for this role with Stalin's knowledge and support, aided by his abilities, energy, and relative youth. The document also notes growing anxiety within Soviet leadership about the future, evidenced by the anti-Zionist campaign, which is interpreted as a sign of fear rather than strength.

input.title: Case of  Poland
input.summary: This document, from September 1960, argues that Western powers have repeatedly failed to uphold their moral principles and treaty obligations in the face of Soviet expansionism, particularly at the expense of Poland. It highlights key betrayals, including the secret agreements at the Tehran and Yalta conferences that effectively handed Poland and other nations over to Soviet control without the knowledge or consent of the Polish government-in-exile. The document also details the Katyn Wood Massacre, in which thousands of Polish officers were murdered by the Soviets, and criticizes Western powers for accepting the Soviet denial and failing to pursue accountability. A U.S. Congressional committee investigated the massacre and recommended bringing the case before the United Nations and the International Court of Justice, but no action was taken. The author concludes that this pattern of moral weakness and political vacillation has undermined Western credibility and emboldened Soviet expansionism globally.

input.title: Orędzie Prezydenta Rzeczypospolitej na dzień Święta Narodowego 3 Maja
input.summary: In a message issued for Poland's National Holiday on May 3rd, 1970, President August Zaleski of the Republic of Poland in exile commemorated the 179th anniversary of the Constitution of May 3rd, 1791, describing it as one of the most uplifting days in Polish history. He highlighted the Constitution's foundational principles, including the rule of law, strong executive power, independent courts, and a standing army, noting that it was widely admired across Europe but threatened neighboring powers who had carried out the partitions of Poland. Despite the heroic efforts of Poles under Tadeusz Kościuszko, Poland ultimately succumbed to its aggressive neighbors, though it continued to fight for over a century until regaining independence in 1918. Zaleski concluded by acknowledging that the Polish nation was once again in captivity but expressed hope that it would draw strength from its thousand-year history.

input.title: Droga życia Józefa Piłsudskiego
input.summary: This document is a catalog for a historical exhibition titled "Droga życia Józefa Piłsudskiego" (The Life's Journey of Józef Piłsudski), held in London from March 13–19, 1970, to commemorate the centenary of Piłsudski's birth in 1867. The exhibition was organized by the Committee to Honor the Centenary of Józef Piłsudski's Birth and featured memorabilia, letters, documents, proclamations, brochures, and photographs drawn from collections held by the Piłsudski family, various private individuals, and Polish libraries and institutions in London and Paris. The exhibition traced Piłsudski's life and work across two major periods: his struggle for Polish independence and the history of the reborn Polish state during the interwar period. The catalog lists numerous display panels covering key stages of his life, from his early years and Siberian exile to his leadership of the Polish Legions and the founding of the independent Polish state. The exhibition was held at Ognisko Polskie, 55 Princes Gate, London, under the honorary patronage of General Kazimierz Sosnkowski.

input.title: Katalog wystawy bibliograficznej poświęconej Józefowi Piłsudskiemu
input.summary: This document is a catalog for a bibliographic exhibition titled "Józef Piłsudski: Writings and Literature About Him," held March 14–19, 1970, at the Polish Social and Cultural Center in London, organized by the Committee to Commemorate the Centenary of Józef Piłsudski's Birth. The exhibition displayed writings by and about Piłsudski, drawn from collections held at Polish libraries and institutes in London and Paris, as well as private collections. Exhibits included Piłsudski's published works, translations, commemorative albums, documents, proclamations, press materials, and caricatures. The catalog includes a preface reflecting on Piłsudski's historical greatness, his legendary status in Polish national memory, and the enduring relevance of his legacy to succeeding generations.

input.title: Orędzie Prezydenta Rzeczypospolitej na 50-lecie zwycięstwa Polski nad Rosją
input.summary: In August 1970, Polish President August Zaleski issued a proclamation marking the 50th anniversary of Poland's victory over Soviet Russia in the Battle of Warsaw. The message praised Józef Piłsudski's brilliant military strategy, which repelled the Soviet forces and protected not only Poland's independence but also that of neighboring nations, while halting the Red Army's advance into Western Europe. Zaleski drew a connection between the 1920 victory and the subsequent events of World War II, arguing that Poland's triumph had temporarily thwarted Soviet imperial ambitions that persisted to the present day. He called upon Poles living in the free world to remain vigilant against Soviet strategic moves threatening Poland's rights and sovereignty. The proclamation urged unity among Poles in their shared political goal of restoring a free and independent Polish Republic, citing the national solidarity of 1920 as an inspiring example.

input.title: Krypta Józefa Piłsudskiego na Wawelu
input.summary: This document, written in London on March 10, 1985, discusses the crypt of Marshal Józef Piłsudski at Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, revealing that during the Stalinist period the crypt was sealed and hidden from communist authorities, yet Poles would secretly gather there at night to pay their respects. After October 1956, the crypt was reopened and veterans of Piłsudski's Legions took on the responsibility of maintaining and honoring the site, organizing independence commemorations and gradually adding memorial plaques, marble tablets, and other patriotic elements despite communist-era restrictions. Key figures such as Dr. Stanisław Korczyński, Colonel Józef Herzog, and others dedicated their efforts to preserving the memory of Piłsudski and the crypt's significance, working in cooperation with Church and state authorities at Wawel. Following Herzog's death in January 1983, stewardship of the crypt and the Piłsudski Mound at Sowice was formally passed to Krystian A. Wałszmundzki and the Citizens' Committee for the Care of the Piłsudski Mound.

input.title: Piłsudski a Solidarność
input.summary: Bogdan Szczeblowski wrote a letter to the Piłsudski Institute in New York on April 18, 1985, submitting an essay titled "Piłsudski and Solidarity" for a competition marking the 50th anniversary of Józef Piłsudski's death. In the essay, he argues that Piłsudski was one of Poland's greatest leaders, whose dedication to independence and use of underground publishing laid the groundwork for later resistance movements, including Solidarity. Szczeblowski draws parallels between Piłsudski's views on Russian imperialism and the oppressive nature of Soviet-dominated communist rule in postwar Poland. He contends that Solidarity's organized, grassroots movement represented a direct continuation of Piłsudski's ideals, particularly in its pursuit of social oversight of government and economic reform, rather than the outright overthrow of the ruling system. Szczeblowski also requests that his address not be made public if the competition results are announced.

input.title: Orędzie Prezydenta Rzeczypospolitej na Dzień Święta Niepodległości.
input.summary: In this proclamation issued on Polish Independence Day (November 11, 1970), Polish President-in-Exile August Zaleski commemorates the restoration of Polish independence on November 11, 1918, after more than a century of foreign subjugation. He recalls how, after just twenty years of independence, Poland was invaded by treacherous neighbors, triggering World War II, and how despite Allied victory, Poland was forced into the Soviet sphere of influence against the will of the Polish people. Zaleski emphasizes that the Soviet Union not only annexed half of Poland's territory but also imposed a communist system on the remainder, threatening European culture and world peace. He calls upon Poles living in the free world to continue the struggle for Poland's renewed independence, as the enslaved Polish nation cannot freely express its own will. The proclamation closes with an expression of faith that, with God's help, full independence will ultimately be restored.

input.title: Karnet Pamiątkowy Stowarzyszenia Polskich Filatelistów w New Britain, CT
input.summary: This commemorative folder was created by the Association of Polish Philatelists in Connecticut, USA, in 1970 to honor the 50th anniversary of the Battle of Warsaw, which took place on August 15, 1920. The battle is historically significant, having been identified by Lord d'Abernon as the 18th most decisive battle in history. The folder, published in both English and Polish, includes a reproduction of a stained glass panel titled "Miracle of Vistula" ("Cud nad Wisłą"), created by Professor of Art Gatti and housed in the Basilica of Loreto.

input.title: Oświadczenie Rządu R.P. w sprawie układu o nieagresji pomiędzy pomiędzy NRF a ZSSR
input.summary: On August 18, 1970, the Polish Government-in-Exile in London issued a statement condemning the non-aggression pact signed on August 12, 1970, between West Germany and the Soviet Union in Moscow, arguing that it legitimized Soviet territorial gains in Central Europe and undermined the freedom of Poland and other nations in the region. The government drew a parallel to the Ribbentrop-Molotov Pact, warning that such agreements with Soviet Russia historically lead to catastrophic consequences. The statement emphasized that any Polish-German reconciliation should be negotiated directly between the two free nations, not brokered through the Kremlin. Separately, on August 15, London's Polish exile community celebrated the 50th anniversary of the Battle of Warsaw with a solemn Mass at St. Andrew Bobola Church, attended by President August Zaleski, Prime Minister Zygmunt Michniewski, and other prominent figures. The government also announced the formation of a Special Commission to coordinate on key political issues and build cooperation with other political centers sharing the goal of restoring Polish freedom and independence.

input.title: Odezwa Rządu R.P. do narodu polskiego
input.summary: On July 7, 1970, the Polish Government-in-Exile in London issued a proclamation to the Polish nation commemorating the 50th anniversary of Poland's 1920 victory over Soviet Russia, a battle in which Poland, under Józef Piłsudski's leadership and with broad political unity, repelled the Bolshevik advance and helped preserve both its own independence and Western civilization. The proclamation drew parallels between 1920 and 1970, noting that Poland once again found itself under the yoke of the same enemy following the 1939 Russo-German pact, with limited effective support from the West. The Government-in-Exile called on Poles to overcome their divisions, unite in common cause, and resist despair, just as their predecessors had achieved a miraculous victory through national solidarity. It urged Poles to honor the anniversary by renewing their commitment to the legal continuity of Polish statehood, as embodied in the Constitution and the President of the Republic, and to work together for the freedom and independence of Poland.

input.title: Polski Nowy Rok w Londynie 1973
input.summary: On January 7, 1973, a traditional New Year's ceremony was held in London at the residence of Polish President Stanisław Ostrowski, attended by members of the Polish Government-in-Exile, military leaders, and representatives of Polish organizations in Great Britain. In his address, President Ostrowski highlighted the 500th anniversary of Nicolaus Copernicus's birth and emphasized the enduring goal of restoring true Polish independence. He discussed key geopolitical issues, including concerns about the European Security Conference, which he viewed as a Soviet attempt to legitimize its wartime territorial gains, and expressed disappointment over the Holy See's decision to end the Polish exile ambassador's mission. Ostrowski also stressed the importance of the 1972 unification of two rival Polish exile political centers as a significant achievement, while acknowledging that the process of establishing a fully representative national body in exile remained incomplete.

input.title: Ratujmy willę Marszałka
input.summary: The villa "Milusin" in Sulejówek, gifted to Marshal Józef Piłsudski by his soldiers in 1923, is in a critically deteriorated state, with mold and structural cracks posing a danger to children attending the nursery school that has operated there for 43 years. A city council commission determined that the building's condition is unsafe, prompting concern from Piłsudski's grandson, Krzysztof Jaraczewski, who fears the villa may collapse before restoration efforts can begin. Earlier in 1999, the city council returned the property to the Piłsudski family with plans to establish Poland's first museum dedicated to the Marshal, allocating 300,000 złoty for the project, but those funds were redirected to other municipal priorities such as water and sewage infrastructure. The mayor of Sulejówek has promised that a new nursery school design will be completed that year, with construction funding included in the following year's budget, though urgent action is needed to ensure the safety of the children currently using the building.

input.title: Polski Nowy Rok w Londynie
input.summary: On January 4, 1970, a traditional New Year's ceremony was held in London, where members of the Polish Government, Council, and various independence organizations gathered to offer wishes to President of the Republic of Poland, August Zaleski. In his speech, President Zaleski reflected on the 25 years since the end of World War II, lamenting that Poland remained under Soviet influence and was not truly independent, with its communist government acting as a foreign authority serving Moscow's interests. He also addressed the broader state of global affairs, noting ongoing conflicts around the world and the ideological divide between the United States and the Soviet Union. Zaleski called for a return to the principles of the Atlantic Charter, emphasizing law, justice, and the right of all nations to self-determination. Prime Minister Aleksander Zawisza also spoke, affirming the Polish government-in-exile's commitment to upholding the legitimate rights of the Polish nation as enshrined in the Constitution of April 23, 1935.

input.title: Przemówienie A. Zaleskiego
input.summary: On October 10, 1970, Polish President August Zaleski opened the fifth session of the Council of the Republic of Poland in London, delivering a speech condemning the communist regime imposed on Poland as a violation of national sovereignty and a system that had failed to deliver social equality while deepening divisions between the privileged and the rest of society. He emphasized that Poland remained under Soviet domination politically, economically, and culturally, and called on the Polish exile community to unite around the legitimate Polish government in pursuit of full independence. Zaleski also commented on the international situation, criticizing the Soviet Union's continued role in fomenting global conflicts and warning Western public opinion about Russia's longstanding imperial ambitions. Prime Minister Zygmunt Muchniewski then delivered an exposé outlining the government's primary goal of restoring full Polish sovereignty and removing Soviet influence from Central and Eastern Europe. He also addressed the recent Soviet-West German non-aggression pact signed in Moscow, offering a cautious Polish assessment that while the recognition of the Oder-Neisse border provided some benefit, the treaty largely served Soviet interests and raised concerns about the exclusion of Poland from decisions affecting it.

input.title: Expose Prezesa Rady Ministrów
input.summary: This document is a 1969 exposé delivered by Polish Prime Minister Aleksander Zawisza at a session of the Council of the Republic of Poland in London, addressing both procedural and geopolitical matters. He outlined the government's planned schedule for council sessions, including a five-week break to allow members time to review government reports and budget proposals for 1970. Zawisza analyzed the internal power struggle within communist Poland between the established leadership under Gomułka and a younger generation of ambitious party functionaries aligned with General Moczar, noting that Soviet support helped Gomułka maintain his position following the suppression of the 1968 student movements and Poland's participation in the occupation of Czechoslovakia. He emphasized that any meaningful political liberalization in Soviet-dominated countries was impossible, as demonstrated by events in Czechoslovakia, and that economic progress in Poland was achieved by Polish society itself despite communist rule, not because of it. The Prime Minister also warned of the long-term Russian ambition to fully incorporate neighboring subjugated nations, as previously seen with the Baltic states, urging greater vigilance from both the Polish government-in-exile and Western powers.

input.title: Wyjaśnienia Rządu R.P. w sprawie rozmów o zjednoczenie.
input.summary: The Polish Telegraphic Agency (PAT) released a statement from the Polish Government in exile, led by Prime Minister Zygmunt Muchniewski, explaining its efforts to reunify the divided Polish political emigration after 16 years of political fragmentation. Since taking office in July 1970, the government established a Special Commission to negotiate with the National Unification Executive, holding several meetings between December 1970 and January 1971 that made progress in rebuilding mutual trust. Talks were temporarily suspended in January 1971 due to an interview given by the head of the National Unification Executive and a separate diplomatic incident, but were resumed after clarifications were provided and the Special Commission was reconstituted under new leadership. The Polish Government reaffirmed its commitment to unifying the emigration under the 1935 Constitution and the authority of the President of the Republic, while acknowledging that some small groups within both factions continued to oppose reconciliation. The government appealed to all Poles worldwide to support its efforts toward Christian reconciliation and unified action toward freeing Poland from Communist rule.

input.title: Posiedzenie Komisji Tymczasowej Okresu Przejściowego
input.summary: On November 17, 1972, the third session of the Interim Transitional Commission was held in London under the chairmanship of B. Podoski, where the key focus was a statement by President S. Ostrowski and an exposé by Prime Minister A. Urbański. President Ostrowski endorsed the Commission's agreed principles as the foundation for unified Polish émigré political action and declared that his presidential term would last until Poland regained independence, but no longer than seven years from the date he assumed office. Prime Minister Urbański presented a constitutional interpretation prepared by a governmental commission, arguing that Articles 24 and 79 of the 1935 Constitution should be interpreted logically in light of Poland's post-war loss of independence, replacing the outdated formula referencing a peace treaty with language tied to the restoration of Polish independence. The exposé also addressed the establishment of a National Representation body to replace the Legislative Chambers, and affirmed the government's commitment to challenging the Tehran and Yalta decisions, including preserving claims to territories such as Wilno and Lwów. The transitional government, representing a broad coalition of Polish independence-oriented political groups, was established to serve until elections for the Council of National Unity could be held.

input.title: Nowy Rząd R.P.
input.summary: On July 21, 1972, the Civil Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland announced the formation of a new Polish government-in-exile in London, led by Prime Minister Alfred Urbański, following the resignation of the previous government under Premier Zygmunt Muchniewski. The new cabinet, sworn in on July 20, 1972, by President Stanisław Ostrowski, included twelve ministers covering key portfolios such as foreign affairs, national defense, justice, and education. In his address, President Ostrowski outlined the government's mission, emphasizing the need to fight for Poland's independence from Soviet domination, unite Polish emigrant communities, and promote democratic values and Christian civilization. Prime Minister Urbański highlighted that the new government represented a historic unification of two previously separate Polish independence emigrant factions after eighteen years of division, with the primary goal of restoring a free, independent, and socially just Poland. The government's first resolution declared the occasion a moment of national reconciliation, bringing joy to Polish émigré society and political organizations alike.

input.title: Przemówienie A. Zaleskiego
input.summary: On April 11, 1970, Polish President August Zaleski opened the fourth ordinary session of the Council of the Republic of Poland in London, delivering a speech condemning the continued subjugation of Poland under Russian imperialism and its imposed communist system. He emphasized that the Yalta Conference agreements were not binding on Poland, as the Polish Government had neither participated in nor consented to its decisions, and criticized Western allies for conceding Polish territory and sovereignty to Soviet influence. Zaleski highlighted Soviet interference in international conflicts across the Middle East, Vietnam, Africa, and Latin America as evidence of Russia's expansionist ambitions, while also noting the economic failures of communist state planning and the hardships faced by young Poles. The speech also marked the 30th anniversary of the Katyn massacre, in which approximately 15,000 Polish officers were murdered by Soviet forces in 1940, with Zaleski calling on those present to observe a moment of silence in their memory. He expressed confidence that Poland's centuries-long tradition of striving for freedom could not be extinguished by the regime, as evidenced by the authorities' need to prosecute citizens merely for reading emigrant press.

input.title: Poland and the Conference on Security  and Cooperation in Europe.
input.summary: This document contains a telegram and two appeals by the Polish Committee for Co-operation and Security in Europe, addressed to democratic governments participating in the Helsinki Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in 1973. The materials argue that Poland's communist government does not legitimately represent the Polish people, as it was imposed through Soviet force rather than free democratic elections. The committee calls for a freely elected Constituent Assembly in Warsaw to determine Poland's political future, with reliable international guarantees to prevent fraud and intimidation. The second appeal, published after the first stage of the Helsinki Conference, expresses disappointment that no participating nation raised the issue of Poland's political transformation, and urges delegates at the subsequent Geneva stage to meaningfully address the self-determination of nations. Throughout, the committee emphasizes that lasting European security and cooperation cannot be achieved without a free, democratic, and truly independent Poland.

POSELSTWO POLSKIE.

Rio de Janeiro, 11 Listopada 1930.

POSELSTWO POLSKIE W BRAZYLII
Otrzymano dnia: 11/XI. 1930.
Nr. 489/100 P.
Załączników:
Załatwiono:

ściśle poufne!

Do rąk własnych Ministra Spraw
Zagranicznych.

DO MINISTERSTWA ZAGRANICZNYCH,

w WARSZAWIE.

W dniu 6/XI. wystosowałem telegram szyfrowany
do Min.spr.Zagr. pod numerem 26, który chcę dopełnić
pewnemi wyjaśnieniami.

Mniej więcej całkowity tekst instrukcyi czy
okólnika rządu francuskiego, zawarty w wyż oznaczo-
nym telegramie /patrz załącznik /, zdołałem otrzymać
przez oddanego sobie specyalnego agenta. - Poprzednio
już z powodu doszłych do mej wiadomości pewnych odez-
wań się niektórych oficerów Misyi wojskowej Francus-
kiej, i wobec przypadkowej rozmowy, jaką miałem z Ge-
nerałem Gamelin o osobie Naczelnika Państwa Polskiego,
byłem na baczności i śledziłem za tem, co się w Fran-
cuskiem działo Poselstwie, z którem mnie łączą jaknaj-
lepsze stosunki. - Rezultatem zachodów było otrzyma-
nie "uboczno" treści rzeczonej, ściśle poufnej in-
strukcyi. - Stwierdzić nie mogłem, czy mamy do ozy-

15
- 2 -

nienia z okólnikiem, czy ze specyalną dla Poselstwa
Francuskiego w Rio instrukcyą. - W pierwszym wypad-
ku Min.spr.Zagr. chyba lepiej od kogo kolwiek będzie
w stanie określić powody, które Rządowi Francuskiemu
mogły podyktować podobny okólnik. - W drugim wypadku
należy szukać przyczyny w okolicznościach specyalnie
lokalnych Riokich. Nad nimi się zastanawiając, nie
mogę nie zauważyć pewnej koincydencyi między datą przy-
jazdu do Paryża w powrotnej z Brazylii drodze, byłego
pełnomocnika ekonomicznego, z datą wyjścia z Quai d'Or-
say rzeczonej instrukcyi. -
Wątpię, aby były pełnomocnik Konsulatu
miał dostateczne stosunki i wpływy w Quai d'Orsay,
aby tam podobno mógł wywołać instrukcyę. - Jest on
jednak posłusznem narzędziem, i ocenionym członkiem
pewnych polskich grup politycznych, mających posłuch
w Quai d'Orsay.
Drugie przypuszczenie moje, wywołały nieraz
nieoględne odzywania się tegoż b.delegata w czasie je-
go tu w Rio działalności i zabiegów o kredyty dla Pol-
ski. - Operował on z wielką nieoględnością i "sans
connaissance de cause". - Dochodziły mnie zapytania,
analiż rzeczywiście "La Banque de France " ma gwaran-
tować Polsce udzielane przez Rząd. lub prywatne finan-
sowe instytucye - kredyty alimentacyjne; podobne za-
pytania niewątpliwie były skierowywanemi i do Francus-
kiej Ambasady. - W razie więc, gdyby te twierdzenia

naszego delegata były nieugruntowanemi, zrozumiałe
zaniepokojenie Rządu Francuskiego i chęć zastrzeże-
nia się przed ewentualnemi nieporozumieniami.
Przypuszczenia te swoje, które na inne mia-

a circular, or a special instruction for the French Legation in Rio. – In the first case, the Min. of Foreign Affairs will probably be better able than anyone else to determine the reasons that may have prompted the French Government to issue such a circular. – In the second case, the cause should be sought in circumstances specifically local to Rio. Confidential

Regarding the matter of relations between Argentina and Brazil.

Santiago de Chile, December 13, 1920.

No. 540/20P.

TO THE MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

C O N F I D E N T I A L

In a confidential report on the departure of South American delegations to the L.N. [League of Nations] meeting in Geneva, I mentioned, among other things, one of the tasks of Dr. Pueyrredón in Europe, namely to find out whether, in the event of an Argentine-Brazilian conflict, a free hand would be granted; in other words, whether one could count on localizing the conflict.

In the meantime, detailed reports from the military attaché Colonel Juan R. Alvelo, the naval captain of the frigate Horacio Esquivel, and the chargé d’affaires in Rio de Janeiro, Mr. Acuña, have reached the Argentine government regarding Brazil's readiness for war and raising doubts about a possible Argentine victory in the event of a conflict.

The diligent work within the Brazilian army and navy and undoubtedly the enormous progress credited to the French Military Mission have influenced a change in favor of Brazil in the balance of armed forces between these two Republics. If Argentina has been militarily superior so far, it is not to such an extent that it could count on a certain victory.

Under these conditions, there can be no talk of an aggressive policy towards Brazil for the sake of using war as a derivative for deflecting from escalating social issues...

Full steam was put into the official side's efforts toward tightening the ties of friendship with the great neighboring Republic, sending as a start the cruiser "9 de Julio", on board of which the Argentine Legation hosted ceremonies in honor of the Brazilians, supporting the actions of private associations for the rapprochement of South American nations, which we had the honor of reporting in the November reports.

Received on: 13/XII 1920

Confidential

Regarding the matter of relations between Argentina and Brazil.

1

Santiago de Chile, December 13, 1920.

No. 540/20P.

TO THE MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

C O N F I D E N T I A L

In a confidential report on the departure of South American delegations to the L.N. [League of Nations] meeting in Geneva, I mentioned, among other things, one of the tasks of Dr. Pueyrredón in Europe, namely to find out whether, in the event of an Argentine-Brazilian conflict, a free hand would be granted; in other words, whether one could count on localizing the conflict.

In the meantime, detailed reports from the military attaché Colonel Juan R. Alvelo, the naval captain of the frigate Horacio Esquivel, and the chargé d’affaires in Rio de Janeiro, Mr. Acuña, have reached the Argentine government regarding Brazil's readiness for war and raising doubts about a possible Argentine victory in the event of a conflict.

The diligent work within the Brazilian army and navy and undoubtedly the enormous progress credited to the French Military Mission have influenced a change in favor of Brazil in the balance of armed forces between these two Republics. If Argentina has been militarily superior so far, it is not to such an extent that it could count on a certain victory.

Under these conditions, there can be no talk of an aggressive policy towards Brazil for the sake of using war as a derivative for deflecting from escalating social issues...

Full steam was put into the official side's efforts toward tightening the ties of friendship with the great neighboring Republic, sending as a start the cruiser "9 de Julio", on board of which the Argentine Legation hosted ceremonies in honor of the Brazilians, supporting the actions of private associations for the rapprochement of South American nations, which we had the honor of reporting in the November reports.

442/20. Ek.
Załączników:

Poufne
IX

W sprawie ewent. kredytów
dla Polski w Brazylji.

7

19/X
20

POSELSTWO POLSKIE.

No 442/20 Ekonom.

ŚCIŚLE POUFNE.

W SPRAWIE EWENTUALNYCH
KREDYTOW DLA POLSKI
W BRAZYLJI.

Do Ministerjua Spraw Zagranicznych.

Na skutek rozmów moich z Ministrem Bertoni,m,
na mocy odezwy Sekcji Handlowej Ministerstwa Przemysłu
i Handlu z dn. 27 sierpnia 1920 r. № 4103/B. podpisanej
przez Szefa Sekcji p. Gawrońskiego, i wobec rozwiązania
Misji Ekonomicznej w Ameryce Południowej, w atrybucje
której nie czułem się w prawie wkraczać, - rozpocząłem
przedwstępne kroki, zmierzające do wyjaśnienia możliwe
ści otrzymania w Brazylji kredytów dla Polski.
Miałem z tego powodu dwie rozmowy z Podsekreta
rzem Stanu M.S.Z. Dr. Rodrigo Octavio /recte Rodrigo
Octavio Lenggaard Menezes/.
W pierwszej, w której zaznaczyłem, że żadnego
polecenia Rządu swego nie mam, i że mówię we własnem
imieniu, dałem mu do zrozumienia, że sprawa przyjęcia
Polsce z pomocą interesuje się kierownicy Spraw Zagrani-
cznych niektórych Południowo-Amerykańskich Republik.

8

II/

zdający sobie sprawę ze światowej doniosłości inicjaty-
wy, w okazaniu pomocy wycieńczonemu walką z barbarją
wschodnią - zwycięskiemu obrońcy cywilizacji światowej,
dla tego męża Stanu, dla tego państwa,co z nią wystę-
piz; że jako jego i Brazylji przyjaciel, wolałbym, aby
ta inicjatywa wyszła od Prezydenta Epitacio Pessoa -
jego przyjaciela. wielkiego druha.
Z doniosłości tej zdawał sobie Dr. Rodrigo
Octavio sprawę.
Co do samego interesu, wskazywałem na formułę,
zastosowaną przy udzielaniu podobnem kredytu Włochom.
Na to odpowiedział, że formuła ta okazała się
*w praktyce niezbyt odpowiednią, że nie dogadza ani Wło-
chom, ani Brazylji, i że pewne braki należałoby uzupełnić
i że obecnie przy pertraktacjach z Holandją wypracowywać
się będzie nowa odpowiedniejsza formuła, którą możnaby
zastosować ewentualnie i do Polski.
Zwrócić trzeba uwagę, że pożyczka, udzielona
Włochom, została przeprowadzona ściśle poufnie /bez u-
działu jakichkolwiek delegatów/ przez Ambasadora Włos-
kiego w Rio de Janeiro. Wyniosła ona 100.000.000 lirów
i była udzielona na 6%; w sprawie traktatu handlowego
i stosunków handlowych z Włochami, przybywa tutaj dzi-
siaj /19-go października/, pod pozorem wręczenia wrze-
nornego listu Króla Wiktora Emanuela, p. Wiktor
Orlando. Bawi też tutaj od dłuższego czasu ks. Aymone
d'Aosta.
Daje nam to wszystko obraz, w jakie ręce po-
wierzają Włochy, swe sprawy handlowo-ekonomiczne i fi-

9

III/

nansowe, i to nie zawsze z pewnemi szansami.
Prócz Włoch, o kredyty ubiega się i Grecja.
Dodam, że należy na czas miesiąca odrożyć wszelkie per-
traktacje z powodu przyjazdu Króla włoskiej Pary Belgij-
skiej i niemożliwości traktowania z Prezydentem Epitacio
Pessoa.
Z rozmowy tej wyniosłem to pocieszające wraże-
nie, że zasadniczo a priori myśli kredytów się nie od-
rzuca.
Dla ścisłości muszę dodać, że w czasie tej roz-
mowy dwukrotnie mnie zapytywał, czy p. Warchałowski i
jego Misja rzeczywiście są rozwiązane i kraj opuściły.
Wspomniał również o wielkich firmach, które
należałoby ująć dla przeprowadzenia zakupów.
W miesiąc później, nie doczekując się wyjazdu
Królewskiej Pary Belgijskiej, byłem powtórnie, pod pozo-
rem powinszowania mu mianowania delegatem Brazylji przy
Lidze Narodów, u Dr. Rodrigo Octavio, i dowiedziałem
się,że poprzednia nasza rozmowa, którą uważałem ze swej
strony za przedwstępną, - dała byka mu asumpt do skrys-
talizowania jej w Memorjale, podanym przez Epitacio
Pessoa, wraz z bardzo życzliwą z jego. Dr. Rodrigo Octa-
vio strony adnotacją. Powtórzyk o konieczności wyczeka-
nia rozwiązania kwestji nowej emisji pieniędzy i wypra-
cowania formuły dla Holandji. W czasie jego , ponoć
trzy miesiące trwać mającego w Europie pobytu, przyj-
dzie się traktować z Ministrem S. Z., który ma zwyczaj
nie odpowiadania i z którym wobec tego mało szans po-
sunęła sprawy naprzód.

10

IV/

Sprawa kredytów, o ile wyczuć mogłem, głównie
zależy od Epitacio Pessoa, od Dr. Rodrigo Octavio, fi-
nansowego doradcy Pessoa - Landsberga, bogatego bankie-
ra niemiecko-polskiego i żydowskiego pochodzenia. Do
niego postaramy się trafić. Jestem już dobrze z jego sy-
nem.
Aby tem więcej zyskać zainteresowania się Dr.
Rodrigo Octavio naszą sprawę, naznaczyłem jurisconsul-
tem Poselstwa Polskiego jego syna i wspólnika w biurze
adwokackim, Rodrigo Octavio filho, czem obu wyrządziłem
przyjemność. Przez syna będę au courant nie jednego,
i nie jedno da się przeprowadzić. Sapianti sat.

Orłowski m.p.
Exp. 20/10-20
K.
